Public Comment

discussions.item: Approval of September 30th, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion to approve the previous meeting minutes was made by Supervisor Cavlli and seconded by Supervisor Kremes. The chair nearly skipped the vote before catching himself. The motion carried on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson presented the budget overview, noting the approximately $235 million budget represents a significant increase over the prior year largely due to inclusion of the highway facility. He described it as a 'status quo budget' and highlighted that net new construction growth of only 1.5% necessitated fee increases. Robinson also flagged a newly announced DNR PFAS community sampling grant with a 20% match requirement that the health department is considering, with the village of Maine identified as an area of particular concern due to impacted wells. Lance, the county administrator, asked committee members to contact his office before Friday at 8:00 a.m. if they wished to propose amendments for the finance committee's Monday meeting. No amendments were proposed by Health and Human Services.

discussions.item: CART and Mobile Crisis Services Expansion
discussions.body: Committee member Katie raised questions about the status of discussions to expand CART (Crisis Assessment Response Team). Lance reported that North Central Healthcare executive director Jason Hake had inquired about CART expansion but that it was not built into the published budget. He noted modifications are being made to increase availability of North Central Healthcare crisis professionals for community response when law enforcement requests assistance. Supervisor John added that discussions with the sheriff's and police departments have shifted focus from CART expansion specifically toward broader mobile crisis service expansion, with a grant funding evaluation ongoing.

discussions.item: 2027 8521 Elderly and Disabled Transportation Grant Application
discussions.body: Staff presented the annual application for 8521 funds supporting elderly and disabled transit services in the county. The county is eligible to receive $366,060 from the state, requiring a local match of $73,201 covered through a partnership with Metroride, North Central Healthcare, and CPZ. Supervisor Ron asked where the local match funds were budgeted, and staff confirmed they are in CPZ's budget included in the 2027 budget before the board. The Transportation Coordinating Committee held a public hearing on October 21st with no public comments received and forwarded the application to this committee. Supervisor Rosenberg moved to approve forwarding the grant application to the county board; Supervisor Foot seconded, and the motion carried unanimously on a voice vote.

publicComment: No public comment was offered.
actionItems: Forward the 2027 8521 Elderly and Disabled Transportation Grant application to the full county board for approval; application due to the state in December.

title: Waterworks Works Meeting
overview: The Wausau Waterworks Commission met on November 4, 2026 and addressed a disappointing DNR lead service line funding award that came in below expectations, leaving an estimated $2 million gap that will require additional borrowing. The commission also approved three items related to a DOT transportation project involving temporary construction easements, a quit claim deed, and a non-reimbursement statement, and received updates on several ongoing wastewater infrastructure projects.

discussions.item: Approval of October 6, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion was made by a commissioner identified as Galhar and seconded by Van Craig. The minutes were approved unanimously with no changes noted.

discussions.item: 2027 Lead Service Line Funding Award from DNR
discussions.body: Director Lynman reported that the city received less DNR funding than anticipated and budgeted for. He explained that the absence of a lead service line replacement ordinance hurt the city's score on a second project, costing approximately $2 million in principal forgiveness. That $2 million will now need to be borrowed as additional debt. Lynman noted the matter will go to the finance committee on November 10th, coinciding with the full council's budget consideration, and may result in a budget amendment for additional borrowing. The chair noted that the alternative is to 'do less with what we've got.'

discussions.item: Wastewater Project Updates: Headworks, Crocker Street Lift Station, Sewer Rehab
discussions.body: Staff member Ben provided updates: the Headworks project is nearing completion with a final completion date of November 15th; the Crocker Street lift station is well underway with the site closed up and asphalt repaved; the Cherry Street lift station project is nearly closed out; and the 2026 sewer rehab project was awarded to Visions, though a project kickoff meeting has not yet been scheduled. No votes were taken on these updates.

discussions.item: Item 3A: Temporary Construction Easements for Parcels 1, 2, 3, and 6
discussions.body: Staff explained the city holds easements over utility infrastructure outside the roadway right-of-way, and the DOT is requesting a temporary construction easement over those existing easements for grading work during the road project. No utility relocation is required. A commissioner identified as Handley questioned why no reimbursement was being sought; staff clarified the city owns no property being given up and will incur no costs, so reimbursement is not applicable. The motion was made by Martins and seconded by Hadley, and the item passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Item 3B: Quit Claim Deed for Parcel 6
discussions.body: Staff explained that on Parcel 6, the DOT is acquiring a permanent limited easement from the property owner for drainage purposes and is asking the city to relinquish any rights it may hold there via a quit claim deed. Staff confirmed the city has no utilities in that area and that the city attorney's office and city engineering have both signed off. Motion was made by Martins, seconded by Hadley, and passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Item 3C: Statement of Non-Reimbursement by Utility
discussions.body: The commission considered a formal statement confirming the utility will not seek reimbursement from the DOT for the transportation project, consistent with the earlier discussion that no utility relocation costs will be incurred. Motion was moved by one commissioner and seconded by Galhar. The item passed unanimously with no further debate.

publicComment: No public comment was offered.

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held its November 4, 2026 meeting primarily to deliberate and act on a conditional use permit for Eau Claire River LLC to operate an aggregate mine and pond expansion at 1320 Kowalski Road. After extensive discussion of operating conditions, noise, flood storage, and future development potential, the commission unanimously approved the CUP 7-0 with conditions. The decision is significant to residents as it sets the stage for potential industrial development of a long-stalled TIF district property by creating flood storage capacity that could unlock adjacent parcels.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: No members of the public came to the microphone to speak during the public comment period. The chair noted no speakers and moved on.

discussions.item: Conditional Use Permit - Eau Claire River LLC, 1320 Kowalski Road
discussions.body: The commission deliberated extensively on the CUP for an approximately 35.58-acre aggregate mining and pond expansion operation. Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick (referred to as 'Nathan' throughout) guided the commission through findings of fact and proposed conditions. Applicant representatives Tom and Gary provided extensive background on the site's history, flood storage engineering, prior interchange planning discussions, the settlement agreement with the Diocese that led to dropping a lawsuit, and confirmed no blasting or asphalt batching plant would occur. After working through roughly 14 proposed condition bullet points, the commission agreed to include conditions on: permitted hours of operation (6 a.m.–7 p.m. Monday–Friday, 6 a.m.–noon Saturday, year-round); a five-year renewal review period; perimeter staking of the excavation area; requiring trucks to be covered to suppress dust and debris; implementation of a reclamation plan; compliance with Village erosion and stormwater control standards; a geotechnical analysis by a qualified engineer to confirm excavation will not compromise adjacent roadways; and compliance with all applicable laws. Conditions on road repair monitoring, specific noise monitoring by either party, and redundant buffer yard language already covered by code were not included.

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items
discussions.body: Following the vote, commissioners discussed scheduling a future educational session on flood district regulations ('Flood District 101') before Eau Claire River LLC returns with a Certified Survey Map to subdivide the nine-acre northern parcel as part of their settlement agreement with the Diocese. Commissioner Dick raised concern that the commission understand fill and flood zone restrictions before approving any future subdivision. Nathan Sandwick also flagged the need to update the village's conditional use permit tracking spreadsheet, which had not been maintained in several years.

publicComment: No public comment was offered.
actionItems: Conditional Use Permit approved for Eau Claire River LLC for aggregate mining at 1320 Kowalski Road with seven conditions: permitted hours (Mon–Fri 6 a.m.–7 p.m., Sat 6 a.m.–noon, 12 months/year); five-year renewal review period; perimeter of excavation area to be properly staked per site plan; trucks to be covered to suppress dust and debris; implementation of a reclamation plan in compliance with Marathon County requirements; compliance with Village erosion and stormwater control standards; geotechnical analysis and confirmation by a qualified engineer that excavation will not compromise structural integrity of adjacent roadways or structures.

Schedule a future commission meeting agenda item (targeting January or February) for a Flood District 101 educational session before Eau Claire River LLC returns with a CSM to subdivide the northern parcel.
Nathan Sandwick to update and maintain the Village's conditional use permit tracking spreadsheet.
Next Plan Commission meeting scheduled for November 16, with zoning ordinance changes carried over for discussion.

title: Economic Development Meeting
overview: The Wausau Economic Development Committee met on November 4th and took action on three substantive items: authorizing staff to prepare a TID 8 project plan amendment for infrastructure projects, approving the $1 purchase of a tax-delinquent property at 108 Myron Street for future affordable housing, and debating a deed restriction and resolution for city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue. The Cleveland Avenue item resulted in a procedural deadlock, with a 2-2 tie on the amended resolution, sending the matter to the full city council on November 24th with section 4 removed from the deed restriction.

Approval of minutes from October 6th, 2026 meeting

discussions.item: Approval of October 6th Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion to approve was made by Alder Neil and seconded by Alder Killian (noted in transcript as 'Kellian'). No discussion occurred and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: TID 8 Project Plan Amendment
discussions.body: Director Fifick explained the amendment would authorize staff to engage a consultant to draft a project plan amendment for Tax Increment District 8, adding infrastructure project costs including lead service line replacement, asphalt overlay, 17th Avenue reconstruction, water and sewer upgrades, and traffic signal replacement. Alder Killian expressed she was not prepared to vote without knowing whether lead line replacement funding covered private or entire replacement, but the motion carried 3-1. Staff noted the item had already been approved 5-0 at the Finance Committee and was placed on the November city council agenda.

discussions.item: Purchase of County-Owned Property at 108 Myron Street
discussions.body: Staff member Tammy presented details on the tax-delinquent property, which has been vacant for years due to a broken pipe causing black mold, rendering it too dangerous to enter. The county approved the city's $1 offer unanimously on October 20th, with full county board consideration set for November 10th. Funding for purchase and demolition would come from Community Development Block Grant funds, not tax levy, with DPW performing the demolition. The end goal is disposition for affordable housing for income-qualifying households. Alder Killian expressed safety concerns about demolition given the black mold but said she would support the motion. Alder Lukans noted for viewers that CDBG/HUD funds, not taxpayer levy money, would be used. The motion carried unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Deed Restriction and Resolution for 1300 Cleveland Avenue
discussions.body: Director Fifick and the committee debated a draft deed restriction prohibiting industrial uses on the city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue, while preserving existing non-conforming uses including Marathon County/Wausau Parks log and wood chip storage and DPW training approved by a 2024 resolution. Alder Tierney's written comments, read into the record by Director Fifick, argued that non-conforming uses should end and the property cleaned up as promised to neighbors. Parks representative Jamie testified that relocating log storage requires council direction on an alternative site of approximately one acre, noting the ongoing Emerald Ash Borer program creates continuous need. Mayor Diny reported that fire training had already been relocated, and miscellaneous DPW equipment and a trailer had been cleaned up. Alder Killian moved an amendment to remove section 4A from the deed restriction, discontinue DPW training by February 1st, and give Parks 6 months to relocate; that amendment failed 2-2. Chair Heniki then moved a narrower amendment to remove only section 4 from the deed restriction, which passed 3-1. The main motion on the resolution as amended then failed 2-2, sending the matter to the November 24th city council meeting with section 4 removed from the deed restriction and a redrafted resolution to be prepared by staff.

title: Board Environmental Resources Committee
overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held its November 3, 2026 meeting, conducting four rezoning public hearings and several town zoning reviews. The most significant action was the committee's decision to postpone a contested farmland preservation-to-low-density-residential rezoning request (MK7 Enterprises LLC in the Town of Marathon) to allow the town additional time to respond, following substantial opposition from neighbors, an attorney representing adjacent landowners, and a local farmer who owns surrounding acreage. Three other rezoning petitions were approved without significant opposition.

discussions.item: 5A1: Weissaki Rezoning - General Agriculture to Rural Estate, Town of Green Valley
discussions.body: Staff presenter Garrett Pogle reported that both the Town of Green Valley and county staff recommended approval. Adjacent property owner William Kaiser raised concerns about an old dump on the property, including potential groundwater contamination and who would bear responsibility. Pogle explained that any new property owner inherits responsibility for existing violations, but that the dump predates the 10-year enforcement window, limiting the county's authority to act. The committee approved the rezoning to forward to the county board.

discussions.item: 5A2: Schultz Rezoning - Rural Residential to Rural Estate, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Pogle reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval of the rezoning. No public comment was offered. The committee approved the motion without notable debate, with Supervisor Drebeck moving and Supervisor Shamborn seconding.

discussions.item: 5A3: MK7 Enterprises LLC Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to Low Density Residential, Town of Marathon
discussions.body: This was the most contested item of the meeting. Attorney Anders Helquist of Weld Riley Law Firm argued on behalf of adjacent property owners that the application failed all four statutory requirements to rezone out of farmland preservation, noting that the applicant's own application admitted two of the four standards were not met, that future land use maps show the parcel as agricultural/woodland, and that there were conflicts with surrounding agricultural uses. Local farmer Tyler Sehafer, who owns surrounding acreage, warned of road infrastructure inadequacy, grain bin noise conflicts, and noted that 100% of approximately 30 residents at a prior town meeting opposed the project. Land surveyor Dan Higinbotham, associated with the project, testified that wetland delineation was underway and soil evaluations were scheduled for the following Tuesday. Additional opposition came from Town of Marathon residents Randall Walcott and Karen Milbeck, who cited misleading communications about the project's intent and concerns about road damage from log trucks. Committee members debated extensively, with Chair Ritter noting a potential inconsistency with how the committee had handled a prior Town of Green Valley case based on future land use maps. Corporation Counsel advised that if a denial motion was made, it needed substantive reasons on the record. A motion to approve by Supervisor Sefelt failed for lack of a second. A denial motion by Supervisor Bro was ruled out of order by the chair after Corporation Counsel indicated it relied on factors not properly before the board (septic suitability). The committee ultimately voted to postpone the matter to no later than the January ERC meeting to give the Town of Marathon an opportunity to respond.

discussions.item: 5A4: Spencer Joint Revocable Trust Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to General Agriculture, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Staff reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval. No public comment was offered. Supervisor Shamborn moved to approve based on findings of fact, conclusions of law, and the town's recommendation; the motion carried without notable debate.

discussions.item: 5B1 & 5B2: Town Zoning Changes - Town of Castle and Town of Weston
discussions.body: Both town-initiated zoning changes were presented by staff as having met all application requirements. Town of Castle sought a partial rezone from farmland to M1 Light Industrial; Town of Weston sought a rezone of Bowman Dairy Farm LLC property from Rural Residential 5-acre to Rural Residential 2-acre. Both were approved by the committee without public comment or significant debate.

discussions.item: 6A1: Data Center Ordinance Development Timeline
discussions.body: Director Lori Mski presented a timeline for developing a data center ordinance following a moratorium put in place in August. Staff described a research and survey phase currently underway, with outreach to surrounding counties and municipalities. The timeline targets a public hearing in June, well ahead of the one-year moratorium deadline, with a committee framework check-in planned at the six-month mark. No action was taken; the update was informational only.

discussions.item: Item 7: 2027 Budget Overview and PFAS Grant Opportunities
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson noted the prior day's budget presentation and reminded committee members that amendment requests were due by noon Friday. Robinson also highlighted two new DNR PFAS grant opportunities: a community-wide sampling grant for private wells and an individual private well sampling program, noting a 20% match requirement that could potentially be offset by in-kind contributions or staff time. Robinson thanked the committee for ongoing work on fee structures given levy restraints.

publicComment: Public comment was incorporated into the public hearings. title: Board (Budget Hearing)
overview: The Marathon County Board held its annual budget hearing on November 2, 2026, receiving a presentation of the proposed 2027 budget from County Administrator Leonard and HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson. The budget features a property tax rate drop of 1 cent to $3.48, maintains current service levels, and is anchored by a no-new-debt funding strategy for the approximately $55 million highway facility relocation from West Street to the Highway 51/Cronin Wetter site. No budget amendments were adopted at this meeting; the board will consider amendments and adopt the final budget at a November 10, 2026 meeting.

agenda.item: Call to order, Pledge of Allegiance, moment of silence, and reading of notice
Roll call
Public comment on agenda items (none signed up)
Budget hearing overview by HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson
Administrator's presentation of proposed 2027 budget highlights

discussions.item: Overview of proposed 2027 budget
discussions.body: HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson outlined the year-long budget development process, noting no amendments had been made since the administrator's September 29 presentation. County Administrator Leonard presented key budget metrics: the property tax rate drops 1 cent to $3.48, Marathon County has the lowest per capita spending and levy rate in the region, and net new construction growth was approximately 1.545%. Leonard emphasized the cornerstone of the budget is shifting the $3.5 million North Central Healthcare payment onto the debt levy to fund the new highway facility without incurring new debt, a strategy he called unprecedented in scale among Wisconsin local governments.

discussions.item: Public hearing on proposed 2027 budget — Flock license plate reader cameras
discussions.body: Two residents testified urging the board to defund the county's Flock Safety license plate reader system, citing mass surveillance concerns, lack of board oversight over the grant contracts, data-sharing with approximately 1,397 agencies across roughly 40 states, and a 2022 contract granting Flock a perpetual license to county citizen data. They asked the board to amend the budget to prohibit county funds — including grant funds — from going to Flock without a board vote, and to require public hearings before accepting future surveillance technology grants. Sheriff Bib subsequently addressed the board, defending the technology as a law enforcement tool with ongoing audits conducted twice monthly by a captain, stating the data belongs solely to Marathon County, that deputies must have an active case number to access the system, and that the department does not use it for immigration enforcement. Supervisor Krebs supported the sheriff's position, comparing it to other law enforcement tools. Supervisor Robinson announced he had arranged a meeting between the sheriff and one of the public commenters to explore resolution. The board agreed to take up the issue in depth at the next Public Safety Committee meeting on November 10.

discussions.item: Public hearing on proposed 2027 budget — Highway facility funding strategy
discussions.body: A resident, a former county board member, testified raising four concerns: the long-term taxpayer implications of Scenario 2A projecting $62.9 million in additional debt levy by 2042, the full $3.5 million shift to debt levy in year one versus the phased approach described in Resolution 4926, and whether proceeds from the Thomas Street, River Drive, and 28th Avenue properties or excess reserves could reduce the $25 million funding gap. Administrator Leonard responded that placing the full amount on the debt levy promptly is necessary to limit the period during which the general fund is being drawn down, reducing the risk of needing to borrow for other capital projects; he confirmed property sale proceeds and post-audit excess reserves would be applied to shorten the interfund loan term. Supervisors Cavelli and Nisth pressed for further detail on phasing options and use of highway reserves, with Finance Director Sam Fensky clarifying the working capital calculation methodology.

discussions.item: Social services staffing — 12 new positions
discussions.body: Supervisor Sundowski questioned the rationale and cost for 12 new positions in the Social Services department. Administrator Leonard and Social Services Director Christa explained that the Children's Long-Term Support (CLTS) social worker positions are fully federally funded through Medicaid billing based on caseload metrics required by the state, that the county is under a corrective action plan obligation to eliminate its waitlist, and that positions will be filled incrementally as caseloads grow. The quality assurance or PCR positions are funded through the state contract stemming from federal requirements and carry no direct tax levy impact; if federal or state funding ends, the positions would be eliminated.

discussions.item: User fees and equity concerns
discussions.body: Supervisor Leur raised concerns that increasing user fees disproportionately burdens lower-income residents and asked staff to track the impact of fee changes on service utilization. Administrator Leonard acknowledged the tension between cost recovery and equity, noted that some fees — such as the marriage license fee — were not increased at the county clerk's recommendation, and stressed that fee and service-level decisions are ultimately board policy choices. He flagged solid waste tipping fees as highly consequential and noted two additional fee items — a professional services fee in the medical examiner's office and minor solid waste changes — would be brought before the board before final budget adoption.

discussions.item: Tax-deed property sale — Resolution 77-26
discussions.body: Supervisor Jensen questioned why the county would sell a tax-delinquent property to the city for $1 when over $75,000 in back taxes and penalties were owed. Administrator Leonard explained that an appraiser valued the property at $0 due to environmental hazards requiring demolition, making cost recovery impossible, and that the city's offer — which does not meet the board's policy requiring the county to be made whole on past-due taxes — was brought to the full board precisely because it falls outside standard policy. The city intends to remediate the property and return it to the tax rolls. Supervisor Robinson noted the county has become more aggressive in earlier title-taking to prevent such situations from accumulating. Supervisor Griner asked whether a part-time position focused on delinquent property recovery would be cost-effective; Leonard suggested the county's existing process has largely caught up and that by 2028 the work would be mostly maintenance.

discussions.item: Educational discussion of November 10 action items
discussions.body: The board previewed several items scheduled for action on November 10, including an appointment of Jennifer Marzu to the Local Emergency Planning Committee, four rezoning ordinances (Town of Green Valley, Town of Marathon, and two in the Town of McMillan), an ATV/UTV ordinance for Highway 34, and two zoning amendment resolutions. Supervisor G flagged concerns about the ATV/UTV ordinance that she planned to raise at the Infrastructure Committee. Supervisors Sandulski and Morash expressed support for the ATV/UTV ordinance based on constituent calls. Supervisor Drew noted that a letter from an attorney regarding the Town of Marathon rezone (MK7 Enterprises) would be discussed at committee the following day. Regarding UW-Stevens Point property, Leonard reported due diligence is underway with the City of Wausau on most buildings through end of Q1 of next year, while the theater building is being pursued for a one-year lease with the Marathon County Center for Arts and Culture ahead of a nonprofit transfer.

publicComment: Three residents spoke during the public hearing on the proposed 2027 budget. The first speaker, who identified herself as the executive director of a domestic violence agency, asked the board to amend the budget to prohibit county funds from being used for Flock license plate reader cameras without a board vote, to require public hearings before accepting future surveillance technology grants, and to seek a corporate counsel opinion on the board's authority and liability. The second speaker argued the Flock system constitutes mass surveillance, cited data showing 464,000 vehicles logged in 30 days with data shared with roughly 1,500 agencies, and found no statistically significant reduction in vehicle theft or property crime attributable to the cameras; he asked for a budget provision barring Flock funding without further study and for the sheriff to implement mandatory audits, quarterly public reports, and limited data-sharing. The third speaker, a resident of Kronau, identified himself as a former county board member and expressed support for the highway facility project and the no-new-debt funding concept but raised concerns about the long-term taxpayer cost of Scenario 2A, the apparent immediate rather than phased shift of the $3.5 million NCHC payment to the debt levy in year one, and asked the board to evaluate whether property sale proceeds and excess reserves could reduce the $25 million funding gap.

title: Common Council Meeting
overview: The Wausau Common Council met on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, taking several significant actions including approving a new full-time human resources coordinator position, passing a data center zoning ordinance, and directing the city to cease use of Flock license plate reader cameras and physically cover them within two business weeks. The Flock camera vote was the most debated item of the evening, with extensive discussion about contract obligations, civil liberties, and the police department's operational role, ultimately passing 9-1 as amended.

discussions.item: Stormwater Utility Study and Stormwater Quality Management Plan Presentation
discussions.body: Justin Gataski of Strand Associates presented a two-part report covering a DNR-approved stormwater quality management plan update and a stormwater utility feasibility study, both funded in part by a $170,000 WDNR grant (50% city, 50% grant). He explained that Wausau currently meets total suspended solids removal requirements but falls far short of the 68.6% total phosphorus reduction required under the Wisconsin River TMDL, achieving only 20.3%. The presentation recommended Alternative 2—a mix of constructing wet detention ponds and water quality trading with neighboring communities—as the best path to compliance. Gataski also outlined a potential stormwater utility charging residents roughly $100–$175 per ERU annually as a more equitable, user-based alternative to tax funding; Alderperson Lukens asked about schools and artificial turf fields under such a system, and Alderperson Hoenecke asked about the top public concerns with implementation, which Gataski identified as resident education about equitable cost reallocation.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda
discussions.body: Two items were pulled from the consent agenda before the vote: File 26-0707 (full-time HR coordinator) and File 26-1013 (Terrace Beautification Special Committee). The remaining consent agenda items were moved by Watson, seconded by Neal, and approved 10-0 without discussion.

discussions.item: File 26-0707: Creation of Full-Time Human Resources Coordinator Position
discussions.body: Alderperson Watson raised concerns about hiring a permanent position before a planned organizational audit, suggesting contracted services as a temporary alternative. Council President Kilian and Alderperson Martens countered that the HR department is severely understaffed and that the position had been discussed and supported by the HR committee unanimously over many months; Martens also noted that the city's annual financial audit flagged the need to capture institutional knowledge. Police Chief (responding to a question about the $10,000 professional development allocation) explained it was drawn from savings generated by bringing crossing guard services in-house. The motion passed 9-1.

discussions.item: File 26-1013: Terrace Beautification Special Committee
discussions.body: Alderperson Larson pulled the item, expressing concern about adding more government committees and raising questions about public health, tree maintenance conflicts, and tall grass. Alderperson Trueblood, whose committee originated the resolution, explained that the current boulevard planting ordinance dates to the 1970s and is vague; the special committee would be temporary, include city staff and citizen members, and use Madison's ordinance as a template. Alderperson Lukens confirmed that the sustainability committee had been consulted and that the committee's role was investigative, not action-oriented. The item passed unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: File 26-0706: Reconsideration and Approval of Data Center Zoning Ordinance
discussions.body: The council first voted 8-2 to reconsider the previously passed ordinance, then debated the main motion. Alderperson Lukens asked whether the ordinance required confirmation of adequate utility capacity; Planning Director Edmonson confirmed the ordinance requires applicants to submit energy service, water consumption, wastewater, and sound reports, allowing the city to deny a conditional use permit if capacity is insufficient. Alderperson Hoenecke raised concerns about industry-funded reports being biased; Edmonson said the city can contract for independent studies at the applicant's expense. Alderperson Martens raised concerns about NDAs, and Edmonson stated she generally opposes NDAs for transparency reasons but deferred to the city attorney on specifics. The ordinance passed 9-1.

discussions.item: File 26-1014: Safe Drinking Water Revolving Loan Program Resolution for Lead Service Line Replacement
discussions.body: The resolution declaring official intent to reimburse expenditures from the Safe Drinking Water Revolving Loan Program for the fiscal year 2027-28 lead service line replacement program was moved by Watson and seconded by Slonski. No discussion was recorded and it passed 10-0.

discussions.item: File 23-1012: Resolution to Cease Use of Flock Cameras (via Suspension of Rules)
discussions.body: The council first suspended the rules 8-2 to bring the item to the floor. Extended debate followed on contract obligations, civil liberties, and operational logistics. Police Chief explained that access to the Flock system could be turned off internally but that cameras—owned by Flock—would continue capturing images stored for 30 days unless physically covered, and that Flock's contract prohibits customers from tampering with hardware. City Attorney Ann confirmed the council has authority to direct the mayor to cease use, but noted the specific wording directing the police department to cover cameras was procedurally awkward. Alderperson Watson successfully moved an amendment directing the appropriate city department, by order of the chief executive officer, to physically cover the cameras within two business weeks; the amendment passed 9-1. On the main motion as amended, Alderpersons Lukens, Tierney, and Martens all cited changed circumstances since the original approval—including documented misuse by law enforcement officers in other Wisconsin cities, Flock selling anonymized data to third parties, and AI-enhanced image processing beyond original assurances—as reasons to act now rather than wait for the contract to expire December 31st. Alderperson Trueblood expressed concern about abandoning the contract and setting a precedent of overriding prior council decisions. The main motion as amended passed 9-1.

publicComment: Five residents spoke during public comment. A resident who identified herself as executive director of a domestic violence agency and chair of the Wisconsin Domestic Violence Fatality Review Initiative urged the council to vote yes on Item 9 to end Flock camera use, citing documented misuse by officers in Milwaukee and Menasha, noting that 42 Wisconsin agencies have ended or decided to end Flock contracts, and requesting written termination notice to Flock by November 15th under Section 11.16. A resident spoke in favor of allowing boulevard planting, describing residents who do so as investing in their neighborhoods, and identifying themselves as a master gardener. A resident urged the council to cover Flock cameras immediately and remove them from the budget, also commenting favorably on the stormwater presentation. A resident urged the council to discontinue Flock camera use immediately and not fund any similar technology in future budgets, calling it a bipartisan issue. A resident urged the council to cover the Flock cameras and remove them from future budgets, citing many things the city needs to spend money on and noting broad public opposition to Flock.

title: Finance Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on October 27, 2026, receiving a clean audit opinion from new auditing firm Maldin Jenkins CPAs for fiscal year 2025, with one minor single audit finding related to suspension and debarment recordkeeping. The committee approved several items including a federal justice grant, a TIF development payment, airport hangar lease increases, and a fire department apprentice program budget amendment, while tabling the Wausau Cemetery Association agreement pending cost estimates and additional information.

discussions.item: Presentation of 2025 Financial and Single Audit by Maldin Jenkins CPAs
discussions.body: Lucas Hand, CPA and director at Maldin Jenkins, presented the city's fiscal year 2025 audit results, reporting a clean, unmodified opinion on both the financial statements and the single audit compliance report. The city ended the year with total net position of $300.3 million, general fund revenues of $46.3 million versus expenditures of $47 million, and an overall net position increase of $12.7 million. One single audit finding was noted — a significant deficiency for suspension and debarment recordkeeping, which Hand described as a common checklist issue with no impact on federal funds. Hand also issued a management point (not an audit finding) recommending cross-training and documentation of key processes, noting that finance department knowledge is concentrated in a limited number of individuals. Alderperson Hincki asked Hand to expand on succession planning concerns, and the chair asked about upcoming GASB standards 103 and 104, with Hand expressing confidence the city is prepared.

discussions.item: Approving Fiscal Year 2026 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant and Interlocal Agreement with Marathon County
discussions.body: Captain Graham presented the annual formula-based federal grant of $15,920, awarded jointly to the City of Wausau and Marathon County, requiring an interlocal agreement for Marathon County to receive funds. The grant is historically used to fund equipment in the regional forensic lab, such as GrayKey or Cellebrite technology. No significant debate occurred and the item was approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Approving Budget Amendment for 415 South 1st Avenue Development Agreement with Gorman Company (Westside Commons)
discussions.body: Patrick from economic development explained that Gorman Company had met all milestones under their development agreement, including minimum spend, project completion, and obtaining 90% occupancy for three or more months, as well as securing permanent financing. The committee approved a $650,000 Tax Increment Grant (TIG) payment to Gorman Company, which will come before the full council as a budget modification. The vote carried without notable debate.

discussions.item: Authorizing Staff to Prepare Project Plan Amendment for Tax Increment District 8
discussions.body: The chair described this item as moving private-side lead service line replacement costs to TID 8 where appropriate, along with 17th Avenue reconstruction and asphalt overlay within the district — topics previously discussed during budget sessions. The motion passed without discussion.

discussions.item: Approving Agreement Between City of Wausau and Wausau Cemetery Association
discussions.body: Staff presented a revised, consolidated cemetery agreement reflecting a current annual payment of $76,721.44 and new language giving the public works director authority to offer surplus vehicles to the cemetery at no cost on a right-of-first-refusal basis. Parks Director Jamie raised significant concerns about a new, large tree removal and stump grinding request from the cemetery — nine trees and 23 total stumps — which would take city urban forestry crews approximately two weeks, raising questions about liability for headstone damage, worker safety on non-city property, and cost. Alder Watson moved to table the agreement until the next finance committee meeting pending cost estimates, a map of the requested work, copies of the prior agreements, and potential cemetery board attendance; Alder Hincki seconded. The motion passed with one nay and the chair abstaining, citing his wife's service on the cemetery board. Items G and H were also pulled to the next meeting.

discussions.item: Approving 3% Increase to Hangar Lease Agreements at Wausau Downtown Airport Beginning 2027
discussions.body: The committee discussed a 3% rate increase for T-hangar leases at Wausau Downtown Airport, with current monthly rates ranging from approximately $3 to $6 depending on hangar size. Staff noted the airport is below market compared to peer facilities. Alder Hincki asked for more detail on how rates are set and how far behind market the city is. Alder Neil moved to approve; Alder Hincki seconded. The item passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Approving Multi-Year Budget Amendment for Wausau Fire Department Apprentice Program Paid by Federal Grant
discussions.body: Fire Chief Jeremy explained this was a bookkeeping amendment to create a budget line matching the previously approved federal apprenticeship grant, enabling staff to track spending across the three-year grant period. He confirmed all costs — including gear, equipment, and collaboration with Northcentral Technical College — are covered within the grant for two cohorts of nine apprentices each. Alder Hincki asked whether apprentices would have a direct path to city employment; the chief clarified they would need to apply for open positions through the standard process. The motion from Hincki with a second from Tyranny passed unanimously.

publicComment: No public comment was offered. The chair noted only staff were present when public comment was called.

title: Community Life & Public Safety
overview: The Village of Weston Community Life & Public Safety Committee met and addressed code enforcement updates, fire/EMS/police department reports, a new liquor license recommendation, and a key vote on a proposed pedestrian crosswalk at Newport Avenue and Business 51. The committee approved recommending a Class B beer and liquor license for Trailside Sports Bar and Grill, and voted to instruct the DOT to include the Newport Avenue crosswalk in design plans for the Business 51 reconstruction project, with one dissenting vote.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Comment
Approval of Minutes from Previous Meeting (September 8th)
Acknowledge Department Reports
Item 5: Code Enforcement Update
Item 6: Fire, EMS, and SAFER Report

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Jim Po, offered public comment. He humorously presented a wooden number five to recognize 6202 Ross Avenue for being on the code enforcement list for five years, calling it 'the pinnacle of commitment to municipal nuisance.' He also raised substantive questions about the proposed Business 51 crosswalk, questioning whether the $60,000 expenditure was a need or a want, how many residents would actually use it, and whether corridor businesses had been consulted or invited to the meeting.

discussions.item: Code Enforcement Update
discussions.body: Staff presented a code enforcement report showing over 100 cases opened annually, with 23 active cases older than one year including one dating to 2021 at a property with abandoned vehicles and solid waste. Code enforcement staff explained the 2021 case involves family deaths and medical issues that slowed compliance, but that the property owner's daughter has been cooperating and making progress this summer. Committee members questioned whether leaving resolved cases open was accurate or inflating case counts, and debated at what point long-standing cases should be escalated to legal action. Staff maintained that as long as progress is being made, they continue working cooperatively rather than pursuing court action, which can be costly and may not address the root cause.

discussions.item: Fire, EMS, and SAFER Report
discussions.body: Fire Chief presented a written report. A committee member asked about mold at Station 2, and Chief confirmed there had been water leaks which are believed to be fixed, with abatement and repair contractors lined up. Omni Glass had conducted exterior assessments and tracked the water intrusion to a second-floor window that was subsequently sealed.

discussions.item: Police Department / Metro Report
discussions.body: Police Chief reported 2,290 calls for service, 54 crashes, and 596 traffic stops. Committee members noted a spike in crashes particularly in the Brill area attributable to highway construction causing frequent lane changes. The Village of Weston recorded 24 crashes compared to 12 in Schofield and 14 in Rothschild.

discussions.item: Humane Officer Training Presentation
discussions.body: Officer Kum Mua, a night-shift officer with approximately 14 years of experience, presented on her 40-hour humane officer certification training through the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection. She described how animal cases differ from typical law enforcement calls in that they require extensive follow-up monitoring and are often subjective, requiring on-site assessment of animals including physical inspection. Chief noted the department has three certified humane officers who handle major cases while other officers manage routine animal calls. Discussion also covered animal registration compliance, with staff noting it is somewhat easier now that registration is handled in-house rather than through a third-party online system.

discussions.item: Class B Beer and Liquor License – Doug's LLC / Trailside Sports Bar and Grill
discussions.body: Village Clerk Pam Bream confirmed online that all required paperwork, background checks, and publication fees had been submitted and a provisional license issued. The committee moved to recommend approval of the Class B beer and Class B liquor license for Doug's LLC doing business as Trailside Sports Bar and Grill. The recommendation will go to the full Village Board at its November 16th meeting for final approval.

discussions.item: Business 51 Reconstruction – Newport Avenue Pedestrian Crossing
discussions.body: Village engineer Mike presented the DOT's planned reconstruction of Business 51, currently scheduled for 2030-2031, and asked whether the committee wanted to include a pedestrian refuge island crossing at Newport Avenue in the design. The village's cost share would be roughly one-third, estimated at $40,000–$60,000 at today's prices. He noted the road median at Newport is currently only four feet wide and people are observed crossing diagonally without a safe refuge. Public works endorsed including it in design. Committee members generally supported it for future-proofing given nearby businesses, apartments, and the junior high school, with one member noting it would set up the corridor for potential future development. One member voted in opposition. The committee voted to direct the DOT to move forward with designing the crosswalk into the project plans.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment in person: Jim Po. He humorously recognized 6202 Ross Avenue for its five-year presence on the code enforcement list and presented the committee with a wooden number five. He also raised concerns about the proposed Business 51 pedestrian crosswalk, questioning the cost-benefit given limited residential density on the west side of Business 51, and asked whether affected businesses had been formally notified or invited to comment. No one commented online or from the audience.
actionItems: Committee recommended approval of Class B beer and Class B liquor license for Doug's LLC / Trailside Sports Bar and Grill to the full Village Board for the November 16th meeting
Committee directed village engineer to instruct the DOT to include the Newport Avenue pedestrian crosswalk in design plans for the Business 51 reconstruction project

title: Parks and Recreation Committee
overview: The Weston Parks and Recreation Committee met to discuss aquatic center repairs and financials, approve the Machm Miller Park master plan, and review the Kennedy Park master plan and quarterly update. The committee voted unanimously to recommend the Machm Miller Park master plan to the Village Board, and held substantive discussion about the future of Kennedy Park development, including the farmers market location, a potential hockey facility in the northwest corner, and fundraising priorities for a future concession stand.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Approval of Minutes from September 28, 2026
Public Comments

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes
discussions.body: The minutes from the September 28, 2026 meeting were moved and seconded without discussion. The committee approved them unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Public Comments
discussions.body: Two public comments were received. Tony Case, a farmers market vendor from Ringle, made three suggestions to improve traffic flow and parking at the Kennedy Park farmers market lot, including widening the entrance to three lanes, adding a permanent directional sign to overflow parking, and exploring use of a strip of land near the power boxes for additional parking. An online commenter identified as Jim criticized the committee sharply, calling out the lack of a Friends of Kennedy Park financial update in the meeting packet, the absence of cost estimates or recommendations in the aquatic center repair staff report, and the failure to include a timeline or realistic financial impact for the Machm Miller Park plan, stating the estimated total cost exceeds $4.137 million and calling the omissions 'unacceptable.'

discussions.item: Update on Aquatic Center Repairs
discussions.body: Staff member Sean reported that contracts are in place with New Pools for leak detection ($12,000) and for motors, pumps, and valves ($123,000-$128,000), both previously approved. Leak detection identified a suspected area near the play structure, close to a previous leak location, and deck removal began to verify it; no cost estimate for repairs was available when the packet was sent Wednesday. Staff explained the pressure-check sonar method used for leak detection and noted the pool has been winterized with RV antifreeze, with water still needing to be returned to the deep well.

discussions.item: Update on Aquatic Center Financials
discussions.body: Sean presented the current operational budget showing revenues of $246,000 against a budget of $226,000, and expenditures of $230,000 against a budget of $256,000, for a positive variance of approximately $16,000 revenue over expenditures compared to budget. The pool special revenue fund balance stands at approximately $29,000, which would grow to $45,000 with the $16,000 surplus, pending remaining utility and winterization costs through December. Staff noted the operational budget does not include capital expenses such as the outside contractor contracts, which run through the CIP.

discussions.item: Machm Miller Park Master Plan and Cost Estimates
discussions.body: Staff presented the most recent version of the Machm Miller Park master plan and cost estimates, noting the plan is not yet approved and there is therefore no current fiscal impact. The total estimated cost is high and the plan is envisioned as a 10-to-20-year roadmap for consistency as committee membership changes. Notable additions from public input included tennis and basketball courts; staff flagged that the cost estimate omits redoing existing walking paths, only pricing new trail sections at approximately $90,000. A committee member moved to recommend the plan to the Village Board, which was seconded by Roger, and the motion passed unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Kennedy Park Master Plan and Quarterly Update
discussions.body: Staff provided a quarterly update noting Friends of Kennedy Park received $17,500 from youth baseball and nearly $4,000 from concession stand proceeds from a softball tournament, bringing the estimated community foundation balance to approximately $124,939.55, with $98,000 dedicated to lights installed at Ray Jack field on October 19-20. The second annual Glow Games indoor event is scheduled for February 20, 2027. Jimmy Olson of the Friends of Kennedy Park addressed the committee, confirming fundraising is ongoing with no brakes applied, and that internally the group sees a concession stand as the next major goal, while remaining flexible given uncertainty about the farmers market location and a potential hockey facility in the northwest corner. Committee members discussed moving the farmers market to the northwest corner near the proposed hockey facility off Altaverie and Newport, which would allow back-to-back ball diamonds to remain and provide a flatter, potentially covered space for market vendors. The committee reached informal consensus that the farmers market will likely remain at field 2 for the next year, the next development step will take more than a year, and fundraising focus should shift toward a concession stand building, with village consideration of phase 2 parking improvements.

publicComment: Two public comments were received. Tony Case spoke in person as a farmers market vendor, offering three suggestions: widening the Kennedy Park parking lot entrance from two lanes to three (one in, two out) to address bottlenecks; adding a permanent mounted sign directing patrons to overflow parking and additional handicap spaces; and exploring a strip of land near the power boxes adjacent to the ball field for 20-35 additional parking spots. An online commenter identified as Jim criticized the committee for omitting a Friends of Kennedy Park financial update from the packet, for providing no cost estimate or recommendation on aquatic center repairs, and for stating 'none' as the financial impact of the Machm Miller Park plan despite estimates exceeding $4.137 million, calling the omissions a failure of customer service to the village's 16,000 residents.

title: Revised Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its October 26, 2026 meeting with six of seven trustees present, taking action on several items including a zoning change request, new municipal center hours, and retaining Ordinance 14-16 as written. Finance Director John provided a detailed TID closure update projecting significant future tax levy benefits, while a public commenter raised concerns about the Green Tree development and well contamination near the project site.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Comment
Staff Reports - Public Works (Greg Allman)
Finance Director/Treasurer's Report - TID Update and Budget

discussions.item: Public Comment - Green Tree Development
discussions.body: Bruny Kramer, addressed the board criticizing the Green Tree development decision, alleging the village did not follow Kronenwetter in-place standards and that no one is accountable for the decision. He also reported that a well service person told him a well on the corner of Pine and Pleasant had 40 feet of contamination and required a full system replacement costing over $10,000, which Kramer said was located near the planned development site.

discussions.item: Finance Director/Treasurer's Report - TID Update
discussions.body: Finance Director John provided an extensive update on Tax Increment District closures, projecting that TID 3 is already in closure mode adding $4,139 to the 2027 tax levy, TID 2 could close five years early in 2029 releasing $80 million in valuation, TID 4 could close two years early in 2032, and TID 1 could close by 2039 with the distribution center coming online. He projected cumulative annual tax levy benefits of up to $400,000-$441,000 once all TIDs are closed, calling it major future benefit to village operations, debt service, and capital projects.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda - Item E (Vouchers/ACH/Credit Cards) and Item F (Operator License)
discussions.body: The board separated the consent agenda after trustee questions. Regarding Item E, Trustee Coyle noted approximately $41,000 in legal costs over 2026 related to open records requests from a specific individual; Finance Director John confirmed the line item on page 13-14 was for one person's requests and pledged a full cost breakdown at the November meeting. Item F, an operator's license application with a missing or incorrect item on the form, was directed back to the clerk for the applicant to correct and resubmit rather than being approved or denied, consistent with prior board practice. Item E was approved 6-0 on roll call; Item F was not voted on and was returned to staff.

discussions.item: Zoning Change Request - 3115 Aspen Road (Boshensky)
discussions.body: The board considered a request by Ms. Boshensky to rezone 2.89 acres at 3115 Aspen Road from R-5 to R-2. There was no notable debate. Trustee Lesniak moved to approve both the zoning change and the accompanying ordinance; Trustee Stowell seconded. The motion passed 6-0 on roll call.

discussions.item: Municipal Center Hours
discussions.body: The board discussed a proposed change to municipal center public hours: 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday, and 7:30 a.m. to noon on Fridays (with staff working internally through 4:30 on Fridays), year-round. Finance Director John raised a concern about December tax collection season and Friday hours but said he would discuss with staff and the administrator before proposing any changes. The board noted that by-appointment access on Fridays has been accommodated previously. Trustee Mortensen moved to approve the new schedule; Trustee Stowell seconded. Motion passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Ordinance 14-16 - Police and Fire Commission Composition
discussions.body: President Joling acknowledged he had made an appointment to the Police and Fire Commission without accounting for the ordinance's composition requirements, resulting in the appointee also serving on the Utility Commission in violation of the ordinance. The board discussed and agreed not to change the ordinance; instead, President Joling will ask the individual (identified as Alex) to choose which commission he wishes to remain on, and a new appointment will be sought for the other. Trustee Coyle moved to keep Ordinance 14-16 as written; motion was seconded and passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Legal Services Renewal - Wolfgram Agreement
discussions.body: Finance Director John presented a proposed renewal of the municipal court legal services agreement with attorney Wolfgram, increasing the rate from $185 to $200 per hour (8.1% increase) locked in for three years. Trustee Solheim raised a concern about the 10-year records retention requirement in Section 5 of the agreement, questioning whether it differed from prior contract language and noting cost implications. The board agreed to table the item and bring it back at the next meeting to allow Clerk Noak time to compare the language with the prior agreement, noting a 60-day termination notice deadline of approximately November 1.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Bruny Kramer criticized the Green Tree development decision, alleging the village failed to follow its own in-place standards, that no one faces consequences, and that a well at the corner of Pine and Pleasant had been severely contaminated, requiring a full replacement costing over $10,000 — located near the proposed development.

title: Committee of the Whole Meeting
overview: The Wausau School Board held a Committee of the Whole meeting on October 26, 2026, covering a range of topics including a charter school update, facilities fee changes, secondary education programming, and a special meeting to adopt the 2026-27 budget and set the tax levy. The board approved a final tax levy of $44,385,271—the same as the prior year—with a mill rate of $6.26 per thousand, 28 cents less than projected at the annual meeting. Key decisions included approving modifications to facility usage fees, tech education course restructuring, and the district's Academic Career Plan.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes
discussions.body: Board President James Bouché sought a motion to approve minutes from September 28, 2026. The motion carried with two members voting in opposition; exact names of those opposed were not stated.

discussions.item: Red Granite Charter School Principal Presentation
discussions.body: Principal Ma Mangan presented on the school's third year of operation as a public Waldorf school, reporting approximately 65 students including 24 new 4K students, 100% teacher retention, and expansion to a second early childhood classroom. Board members, including one identified as Pat McKee, praised word-of-mouth marketing and noted the school's no-screen and outdoor-focused approach as enrollment drivers. The board asked questions about space and what drove the enrollment increase but took no formal action.

discussions.item: Audit of the Bills
discussions.body: Bouché sought a motion to approve the audit of bills as presented in board books. The motion carried with opposition noted but not counted by name.

discussions.item: Facilities Usage Fee Schedule - Phase One Modifications
discussions.body: Assistant Superintendent Dr. Elizabeth Channel and Buildings and Grounds Director Ryan Ormansky presented a first phase of modifications allowing 501(c)(3) organizations, Title 36 youth groups (such as scouts), and governmental agencies to request fee waivers for facility use during normal operating hours (6:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.). A board member noted the importance of stewardship of taxpayer-funded buildings while supporting community partnerships. The motion to recommend the first phase to the full board carried.

discussions.item: Legal Counsel Expenses Q1 2026-27 (Informational)
discussions.body: Dr. Channel confirmed no additional information beyond what was in board books; no action was taken on this written informational report.

discussions.item: Hmong Language Offering
discussions.body: Director of Secondary Education Dr. John Tossky and Dr. Cwell presented findings on potentially offering Hmong as a language course, noting highlights such as community engagement, college credit potential, and innovative positioning, as well as challenges including declining enrollment in existing global languages, difficulty finding and retaining a licensed Hmong teacher (no licensure programs exist in Wisconsin for the DPI 1389 license), and curriculum development costs. Board members Charles Burger and others asked about Wave virtual delivery, summer program pilots, and demand measurement. Lance Trollop and Pat McKee cautioned that adding a language amid declining enrollment and budget constraints could come at the expense of existing language offerings. Board President Bouché noted Act 31 obligations regarding Southeast Asian heritage language instruction. The board directed staff to gauge student interest before the next presentation on this topic; no vote was taken.

discussions.item: Tech Ed Course Approvals - Digital Design and Manufacturing
discussions.body: CTE Coordinator John Wy presented a restructuring of the graphics and Fab Lab pathways, combining Graphics 1 and Fab Lab into a new 'Digital Design and Manufacturing' course, renaming Graphics 2 to 'Graphic Design and Software,' and reducing Graphics 3 (Warrior/Lumberjack Graphics) from a double block to a single block while retaining NTC dual credit. Teachers and administration were reported to be fully supportive. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried.

discussions.item: Academic Career Plan (ACP) 2026-27
discussions.body: CTE Coordinator John Wy presented the district's ACP in alignment with PI26, highlighting student success stories, innovative pathways including aviation, robotics, auto collision, and math and construction, and two goals: expanding work-based learning participation by 10% and reducing undecided seniors from 11-15% to under 8%. Board members praised the presentation and noted the importance of ACP for community awareness. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried.

discussions.item: Annual Student Fees 2027-28
discussions.body: Dr. Kempky reported no increases to student fees for 2027-28, noting ongoing monthly collaboration with Dr. Channel and athletic directors on athletics funding. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried with opposition noted.

discussions.item: Special Meeting: Final 2026-27 Budget Adoption and Tax Levy
discussions.body: Dr. Channel presented the finalized 2026-27 budget, reporting a mill rate of $6.26 per thousand—28 cents less than projected at the annual meeting—driven by increased equalization aid and increased property values. Enrollment declined by 215 students from fall 2025 to fall 2026, with a three-year rolling average down 133 students. The district is approximately $13 million behind inflationary pace, representing a cumulative $71 million deficit since 2011. The private school voucher aid deduction totals $4,629,595, adding about $65 per $100,000 home. The board approved the final budget and set the tax levy at $44,385,271—the same as the prior year—while defeasing approximately $11 million in debt. A board member requested additional data on equalized value trends, transportation reimbursements, and special education enrollment for use in legislative discussions.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #4 Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its fourth budget session on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, working through the 2027 budget with numerous amendments. The committee approved the 2027 budget as amended by a 4-1 vote, with key changes including removal of $50,000 in Flock ALPR camera funding (redirected to general fund street maintenance or public safety motorpool), removal of $150,000 for a city administrator position (redirected to council consulting services for a pending city audit), and removal of several deferrable capital items. The amended budget recommendation will advance to the full Common Council for a public hearing on November 10th.

agenda.item: Call to Order
Public Comment on Agenda Items
Discussion and Possible Action: Recommending 2027 Budget Including Setting 2027 Fee Schedule
Staff Update: Flock Invoice Timing and 2026/2027 Budget Implications
New Property Record Maintenance Fees Presented by Assessor Rick Rubo
Updated Assessed Value and Tax Rate Presentation
Motor Pool Budget Reconciliation
Capital Budget, Debt Service Scenarios, and TID 8 Project Plan Amendment Discussion
Budget Amendments and Votes

discussions.item: Public Comment on Flock ALPR Cameras
discussions.body: Five members of the public spoke during public comment, all urging the committee to remove Flock ALPR camera funding from the 2027 and 2028 budgets. Speakers cited privacy concerns, the risk of the system being used as a stalking tool, ongoing litigation in Wisconsin against municipalities using Flock data, and the argument that nonappropriation carries minimal legal risk. One speaker detailed the specific budget line changes needed and noted the Public Health and Safety Committee had voted 5-0 the prior evening to recommend removing the Flock funding.

discussions.item: New Property Record Maintenance Fees
discussions.body: City Assessor Rick Rubo presented new proposed fees for property record maintenance and parcel splits/combinations, noting about 12 Wisconsin municipalities have adopted similar fees. Rubo explained that the city currently receives no reimbursement for significant staff time involved in updating physical and electronic assessment records when permits are issued or parcels are split and combined, citing a 50-unit condominium project as an example of the administrative burden. The committee later approved these new fees by voice vote.

discussions.item: Updated Assessed Value and Tax Rate Impact
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne reported that the final assessed value came in at a 2.56% increase — significantly stronger than the estimated 1% — bringing the total to approximately $464,994,200. This revised the projected 2027 tax rate down from an estimated $9.24 to $9.10 per thousand, reducing the estimated tax impact on a $200,000 home from $9,973 to $7,152. The committee noted the city is still awaiting apportionment figures from the county and school district.

discussions.item: Motor Pool Budget Reconciliation
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne presented a motor pool reconciliation showing general fund department budgets totaling approximately $4,018,000 and entity-wide totals of $4.5 million, against projected motor pool revenues of $4.8 million and budgeted expenses plus capital purchases leaving a shortfall of $448,000. She noted a target of an additional $1.3 million would be needed to fully recover costs, but that strong 2026 general fund performance would likely allow a budget modification to true up the capital and support the full fee structure for both 2026 and 2027.

discussions.item: Capital Budget, Debt Service Scenarios, and TID 8 Discussion
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne presented three debt service scenarios (flat 10-year, structured 10-year, and 15-year) for proposed 2027 and 2028 infrastructure borrowing, noting that a structured 10-year amortization would best control levy growth. She also presented a proposal to amend TID 8's project plan to include 17th Avenue design ($250,000), asphalt overlay ($300,000), and up to $2.5 million for lead service line replacements, potentially allowing the district to close as early as 2035. Alderperson Hoenecke and others raised questions about balancing essential capital needs against deferrable projects, with Hoenecke advocating for stricter scrutiny of non-essential borrowing.

discussions.item: Alcohol and Licensing Fee Amendments
discussions.body: City Clerk staff presented proposed changes to the alcohol and licensing fee schedule, noting most fees are capped by state statute. Proposed changes included a new $100 late publication fee and a $150 late fee to encourage timely license renewals, a reduction of the group publication fee from $30 to $25, an increase in the lapsed bartender license fee from $125 to $130, a reduction of the alcohol premise amendment fee from $150 to $25 to improve enforceability, and an increase in the Class A beer license from $350 to $400. Alderperson Tierney moved to adopt the revised alcohol and cigarette license fees as advised by staff; seconded by Watson, approved unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Flock Camera Funding Removal Amendment
discussions.body: Alderperson Tierney moved to remove $50,000 for Flock cameras from the 2027 budget and an equivalent amount from the 2028 budget, seconded by Watson. Discussion centered on where to redirect the $50,000, with the finance director suggesting it could be moved to the general fund to support motor pool line items in police, fire, or street maintenance. Mayor Diny recommended keeping the funds within public safety for items such as crowd control barricades. The motion as amended to redirect the funds within the general fund to street maintenance or public safety passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: City Administrator Funding Removal Amendment
discussions.body: Alderperson Tierney moved to remove $150,000 budgeted for a city administrator and redirect it to the council's consulting services line item to fund a previously approved city audit. Alderpersons Watson and Hoenecke expressed support for redirecting the funds toward the audit rather than eliminating them entirely, noting a council resolution authorizing the audit had passed the prior week. After discussion about whether to place funds in reserve (which would require a two-thirds vote to access), the committee agreed to move the $150,000 to council consulting services. The amendment passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Alley Paving Removal Amendment
discussions.body: Alderperson Tierney moved to remove $45,000 for alley paving, seconded by Hoenecke. Public Works Director clarified that this funding is only used when residents petition for new alley paving — the city currently has no petitions for 2027 — and that removing it would only require any future petitioners to wait until the 2028 budget. Alderperson Neal withdrew a suggestion to retain $15,000 for the most critical needs after the director's clarification. The amendment passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Tree Planting Removal Amendment
discussions.body: Alderperson Hoenecke moved to remove $25,000 for street tree planting, seconded by Watson for purposes of debate. Parks staff clarified that this budget replants trees on reconstructed streets — specifically 11th Avenue and Ethel Street for 2027 — and that improved planting techniques using root collars reduce sidewalk damage. Alderpersons Neal, Martens, and Watson spoke strongly against removal, citing community character, property values, environmental benefits, and a duty to residents whose trees were removed during prior reconstructions. Hoenecke clarified he was not opposed to trees but objected to incurring 10-year debt for $25,000; he said he would support funding it from cash. The motion failed 4-1, with Hoenecke casting the only yes vote.

discussions.item: TID 12 Tool/Design Engineering Removal Amendment
discussions.body: Alderperson Tierney moved to remove $150,000 for Forest Street two-way conversion design engineering from TID 12, seconded by Hoenecke. City Engineer Alan explained the study would design roundabout and signal changes needed to convert First Street and Forest Street to two-way traffic following removal of the State Highway 52 designation. The committee noted TID 12 is still in early increment years and fiscally fragile, having recently relied on a donor amendment from TID 7. The motion passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: TID 8 Capital Project Reallocation Amendment
discussions.body: Chair Martens moved to reallocate $250,000 for 17th Avenue design, $300,000 for asphalt overlay, and up to $2.5 million for lead service line replacements from the general capital projects fund into TID 8, seconded by Hoenecke. Finance Director Maryanne noted this would reduce the debt service levy but not total borrowing. The amendment passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Final Vote on 2027 Budget as Amended
discussions.body: After all amendments were acted upon and a withdrawn motion to use reserves to offset borrowing, the committee voted on the 2027 budget as amended. The budget passed 4-1, with Hoenecke casting the lone no vote. The recommendation will proceed to a Common Council public hearing on November 10th. The committee was also informed that auditors will present 2025 financial results at the next Finance Committee meeting and that financial advisors from Ehlers may also attend.

publicComment: Five residents spoke during public comment, all addressing Flock ALPR camera funding. The first speaker asked the committee to remove Flock camera funding from the budget on grounds of privacy and misuse of resources. A second speaker endorsed the first speaker's comments without elaborating. A third speaker, identifying themselves as working in domestic violence prevention, argued that ALPR systems pose a stalking risk to survivors, cited documented cases of officer misuse nationwide, detailed the specific budget line changes needed to remove the Flock funding, and argued that litigation risk from leaving the contract is greater than from exercising the nonappropriation clause. A fourth speaker expressed community support for removing the cameras based on social media sentiment and urged the city not to renew or replace any ALPR contracts. A fifth speaker said the removal would help rebuild constituent trust and represents a fiscal savings.

title: Board Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors met on Tuesday, October 20, 2026 and took several significant votes, most notably approving Resolution 68-26 as amended to authorize Phase 4 construction of the new highway facility in Kronenwetter at a guaranteed maximum price of approximately $55 million. The board also appointed Aaron Griner as Infrastructure Committee Chair, passed an Operation Greenlight resolution honoring veterans, approved a Child Support Agency budget amendment, and adopted a resolution calling for reconsideration of proposed federal census residency rules.
