discussions.item: Award Presentation to Regional Forensic Science Center
discussions.body: Greg Kimble of American Tissue Services Foundation presented a certificate and teardrop award to the Marathon County Medical Examiner's Office, noting that in the coming year over 600 people would benefit from tissues recovered with the office's assistance and that 57.8% of Marathon County residents are registered organ donors, above the state average of 55.7%. Katie Shara of the Lion's Eye Bank of Wisconsin presented the 2026 Crystal Vision Award to the Medical Examiner's Office for outstanding commitment to eye donation. Representatives of the Medical Examiner's Office, including autopsy supervisor Nick Hanky and medical legal investigator Leah Shite, accepted both awards.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda Items C9 through C13E
discussions.body: Supervisor Drebeck moved and Supervisor Conway seconded approval of consent agenda items C9 through C13E. The motion carried but was not unanimous, with no discussion recorded.

discussions.item: Infrastructure Committee Chair Appointment – Aaron Griner
discussions.body: The board considered appointing Aaron Griner as Infrastructure Committee Chair to complete a term expiring at the April 2028 organizational meeting, replacing Chris Dickinson. Griner delivered a lengthy statement emphasizing his commitment to data-driven deliberation, fiscal responsibility, and preparing the county for novel infrastructure challenges including transportation, energy, data processing, and AI development. The motion by Supervisor Watson, seconded by Supervisor Gao, carried but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: Resolution 68-26: Phase 4 Construction of New Highway Facility
discussions.body: The board engaged in extensive debate over the approximately $55 million guaranteed maximum price for a new highway facility in Kronenwetter. Supervisor Sandalski offered a successful amendment requiring the board to develop a property divestment strategy for the existing West Street site aimed at returning property to the tax rolls and applying proceeds to the general fund. Highway Commissioner Lang and project manager Chris Hullman detailed operational benefits including indoor equipment storage to extend vehicle lifespans, improved wash bay capacity, and geothermal HVAC with an estimated $760,000 federal tax credit on the $1.9 million borefield. County Administrator Leonard emphasized that the $54,981,000 figure is a guaranteed maximum price under construction management at risk, that no bonding is planned, and that construction costs have risen significantly over years of delay — citing a comparable Sauk County highway shop approved in 2022 for $50 million. Opponents including Supervisors Straw, Hapa, and Drop raised concerns about the total cost, coal dust drift from the nearby Weston power plant, and traffic access. Supervisor Mask called the question, which passed, ending broad debate. The resolution as amended was approved but not unanimously.

discussions.item: Resolution 71-26: Operation Greenlight
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs explained that Operation Greenlight, started approximately five years ago by NACo, calls for turning lights green during Veterans Week to recognize veterans' service. Moved by Supervisor Cavelli and seconded by Supervisor Morash, the resolution passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Resolution 72-26: Child Support Agency Budget Amendment
discussions.body: The board considered a budget amendment to recognize additional FY2024 state performance incentive funds for the Child Support Agency. Because it is a budget amendment, a two-thirds majority was required. Moved by Supervisor Gao and seconded by Supervisor Robinson, the resolution carried but was not unanimous, with no discussion recorded.

discussions.item: Resolution 73-26: Reconsideration of Proposed Census Residency Rules
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson explained that proposed federal census rule changes would use January through April 1 presence — rather than tax home — to determine residency, potentially reclassifying Wisconsin snowbirds as residents of southern states and reducing the state's share of $2.8 trillion in federally allocated funds. Supervisor Pool clarified that the resolution is narrowly focused on the residency definition and not broader census changes. Moved by Supervisor Griner and seconded by Supervisor Nisth, the resolution carried but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: Motion to Reconsider Consent Agenda Item 13C1 (ARPA Funds Reclassification to Forensic Science Center)
discussions.body: Supervisor Straw moved, seconded by Supervisor Hapa, to reconsider the consent agenda item reclassifying excess ARPA funds to the completed forensic science center project. Administrator Leonard explained that Treasury guidance requires ARPA funds to be allocated to previously identified projects by December 31, 2024, and that reclassifying the funds to the forensic science center — rather than returning them to the federal government — would free up already-spent county dollars to flow back into the capital improvement plan for future board use. Supervisor Robinson warned of potential federal clawback if funds were spent on non-identified projects. The motion to reconsider was defeated.

title: Board Human Resources, Finance & Property Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board Human Resources, Finance & Property Committee met and acted on several property and budget matters, including directing two tax-deeded Edgar parcels to be re-listed on Wisconsin Surplus with a $500 minimum opening bid, approving a $1 sale of a condemned Wausau property to the city, and advancing a resolution on 2030 census residency rules. The committee also forwarded a resolution authorizing construction of the new county highway facility to the full county board for action that same evening.

Approval of Minutes — October 7th and 12th meetings
5B3 — Discussion of county-owned parcels in Village of Edgar (tax-deeded properties)
5B1 — Update on highway project bids and consideration of resolution to proceed with construction (Resolution 68-26)
5B2 — Budget amendment to accept additional child care support funding from State of Wisconsin
5B4 — Consideration of offer to purchase county-owned parcel at 108 Myron Street, City of Wausau

discussions.item: Public Comment — Edgar Tax-Deeded Parcels
discussions.body: Dwayne Warner of Edgar appeared to express interest in two back-tax parcels in the Village of Edgar, explaining he owns surrounding property and that the land — consisting of creek bed and swamp — is not developable. He noted the Village of Edgar administrator indicated the village wanted to return the parcels to him to consolidate ownership. His public comment directly preceded and informed the committee's subsequent action on agenda item 5B3.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes — October 7th and 12th Meetings
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs moved to approve the minutes of the October 7th and 12th meetings. A supervisor identified as 'Nis' (likely Nisl or similar) seconded. No discussion was held and the motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: 5B3 — County-Owned Parcels in Village of Edgar
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard outlined four options for two narrow, undevelopable tax-deeded parcels: sell to the Village of Edgar for its $100 offer, negotiate directly with adjacent owner Dwayne Warner, entertain a third interested party on one parcel, or re-list on Wisconsin Surplus at a lower starting price. The presiding officer favored re-listing on Surplus to avoid favoring one party. A motion was made to re-list both parcels on Wisconsin Surplus for 30 days at a $500 opening bid per parcel, with the matter returning to the board if unsold. It was noted that the county's back-tax costs ($568 and $440 respectively per parcel) would likely be a wash at the $500 price. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: 5B1 — Highway Facility Construction Resolution (Resolution 68-26)
discussions.body: The committee considered Resolution 68-26 authorizing staff to proceed with Phase 4 construction of the proposed new county highway facility. Highway Commissioner Kevin [last name inaudible] confirmed that bids had been received and validated, and that the guaranteed maximum price figure in the resolution represents a ceiling — actual costs may come in lower. Chair Gibbs moved to approve the resolution and forward it to the full county board for consideration that evening. The motion carried unanimously with no notable opposition.

discussions.item: 5B2 — Budget Amendment: Additional Child Care Support Funding
discussions.body: Staff member Kristen [last name inaudible] presented a straightforward budget amendment to accept $12,582 in additional state child support funding earned through strong 2024 performance by the county's child support unit. Chair Gibbs moved to approve the amendment and forward it to the full board; Vice Chair Pool seconded. The motion carried unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: 5B4 — Offer to Purchase 108 Myron Street, Wausau ($1 Sale to City)
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard explained that the county-owned property at 108 Myron Street has an appraised value of $0 due to interior mold and hazardous conditions, with an estimated demolition cost of up to $25,000. The City of Wausau offered $1 to acquire the property, demolish the building, and return the land to housing use through its Community Development Authority. Corporation counsel noted that under Wisconsin Chapter 292, the county as a tax-delinquency acquirer is exempt from environmental liability upon transfer. Chair Gibbs raised concern about ongoing environmental responsibility; counsel and the administrator clarified that liability transfers with the sale on an as-is basis. The motion to accept the $1 offer passed with one abstention.

discussions.item: 5B5 — Resolution on 2030 Census Residency Rules
discussions.body: The presiding officer introduced a resolution opposing proposed federal changes to census residency rules (Chapters 60 and 70 of the Code of Federal Regulations) that would count Wisconsin snowbirds as residents of southern states where they winter, potentially costing Wisconsin a congressional seat and reducing its share of $2.8 trillion in federally allocated funding. Chair Gibbs noted NACO is also engaged on the issue. Supervisor [name inaudible] expressed support but wanted to confirm the resolution was narrow in scope — focused only on residency counting — before agreeing. The public comment period on the federal rule closes November 2nd. The motion to approve the resolution and forward it to the full board carried unanimously.

discussions.item: 5B6 — Resolution: Operation Greenlight
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs described Operation Greenlight as a five-year-old program originating in New York that encourages municipalities to illuminate buildings in green during Veterans Week (November 4–11) to honor military veterans and raise awareness of services provided through the county's CVSO and the VA. A supervisor identified as 'Nisth' moved to support Resolution R71-26; Vice Chair Pool seconded. The motion carried unanimously with no opposition.

discussions.item: 5B7 — Transfer of Property Adjacent to Highway Q
discussions.body: Highway Commissioner Kevin explained that the parcel appears to be old road right-of-way from a previous alignment of Highway 29, resulting in confused joint ownership with the town. The town agreed to accept a quitclaim deed, and county staff ensured Highway Q right-of-way was preserved in the CSM. The item had already been approved by the Infrastructure Committee. A supervisor moved to transfer the property; Chair Gibbs seconded. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: 6A — Year-to-Date Budget Update
discussions.body: Finance staff member Sam presented the year-to-date budget through July, noting the county is at 58.3% (7/12ths) of the year with payroll at 54.41% benchmark. Areas flagged for monitoring include Clerk of Courts professional services (likely to exceed budget due to court-ordered evaluations), Corporation Counsel legal fees (expected to be covered by the North Central Healthcare intergovernmental agreement), DA revenue shortfalls from discovery fee changes, and the Medical Examiner's first year of operations. Chair Gibbs praised the finance department's improved reporting and raised questions about the administrative burden of federal changes; staff noted the state has largely protected the county from shortfalls through legislative fixes, though impacts on North Central Healthcare charity care remain a longer-term concern.

discussions.item: 6B — 2027 Budget / Airport Minimum Revenue Guarantee
discussions.body: Vice Chair Pool raised questions about the $150,000 annual levy for the airport minimum revenue guarantee program, noting the 2026 funds had not yet been deployed and asking whether they would roll over. Administrator Leonard explained that Synergy has secured community matching pledges and a revised fund management agreement is being finalized for transfer of the 2026 funds to Synergy; a $950,000 Small Community Air Service Development Grant was recently awarded for Detroit route expansion. The administrator indicated he does not expect a rollover of the 2026 $150,000 and suggested the board evaluate 2027 funding after the budget is adopted. The 2027 proposed budget was confirmed to have been published in the Wausau Daily Herald as required.

He explained he owns surrounding property and sought to consolidate the land into one contiguous parcel, noting the land is undevelopable creek bed and swamp. He stated the Village of Edgar administrator indicated the village simply wanted to return the parcels to him.

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Plan Commission met on October 20, 2026 and approved five action items, including the landmark designation of Yawkey Park, a rezoning at 909 South 60th Avenue from medium to heavy industrial, a preliminary plat for the West Hill First Addition subdivision, and two alley/road vacations. The Yawkey Park landmarking, supported by public comment from the Yawkey family heirs and a unanimous Historic Preservation Commission vote, will advance to City Council for final approval.

agenda.item: Call to Order
Public Comment
Consideration of Minutes – September 15, 2026 Regular Meeting
Item E (moved up): Potential Landmarking of Yawkey Park
Public Hearing: Rezoning of 909 South 60th Avenue from Medium Industrial to Heavy Industrial
Item 4A: Rezoning 909 South 60th Avenue – Medium Industrial to Heavy Industrial
Item 4B: West Hill First Addition Preliminary Plat

discussions.item: Public Comment – Yawkey Park Landmarking
discussions.body: Two speakers addressed the commission. Kathy Foley read a statement on behalf of the Yawkey family heirs — great-grandchildren Alice Woodson Smith, A. Woodson Haigie, Abigail Spire, Lee Tuckey, and Nancy Lee Fischer — expressing full support for designating Yawkey Park as a historic landmark and calling for protection of its 106-year-old footprint 'deeded for use by the public in perpetuity.' Christine Martins noted she authored the nomination document and that the Historic Preservation Commission had already passed it unanimously with no opposition at the public hearing stage.

discussions.item: Consideration of Minutes – September 15, 2026
discussions.body: A motion to approve the September 15, 2026 minutes was made by Bruggeman and seconded by Balkin. No corrections were offered and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: Potential Landmarking of Yawkey Park (Item E, moved up)
discussions.body: The mayor moved this item up on the agenda to accommodate attending citizens. A motion to approve was made by Bruggeman and seconded by Balkin with no discussion. The commission approved the landmarking unanimously by voice vote; the mayor noted the measure would proceed to City Council for final action.

discussions.item: Rezoning of 909 South 60th Avenue – Medium Industrial to Heavy Industrial (Item 4A)
discussions.body: Assistant City Planner Edmonson explained that the parcel is surrounded by heavy industrial uses and natural features that buffer it from other development, and noted that a neighboring parcel to the north had recently received a similar rezoning. Staff found no concerns with the application and recommended approval as consistent with surrounding properties. The commission approved the rezoning unanimously by voice vote; the mayor confirmed it would go to November City Council.

discussions.item: West Hill First Addition Preliminary Plat (Item 4B)
discussions.body: Planner Lenz explained the preliminary plat covers a new subdivision west of Stettin Elementary School, with Arborvitae Drive designed to connect to the adjacent Greentree subdivision to the west. The INF Committee had previously recommended approval unanimously. The commission approved the preliminary plat unanimously; the developer will return with a final plat for the phase-one lots.

discussions.item: Vacating and Discontinuing Alley Bounded by Lakeview Drive, Bertha Street, Elmwood Boulevard, and Midway Boulevard (Item 4C)
discussions.body: The mayor described the alley as an unpaved grass strip with limited use and no garage access dependency. All adjacent property owners except 2514 signed a petition to vacate, and a utility easement would remain in place. The INF Committee had previously recommended approval. The commission approved the vacation unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Vacating and Discontinuing 134-ft Southerly Extension of Liberty Ridgeway (Item 4D)
discussions.body: Commissioner Trueblood explained that Liberty Way continues to the east and north, making this southern stub an undeveloped dead end; a large home is being constructed in the area, making vacation appropriate. He stated he 'strongly advised' approval. A utility easement will remain. The commission approved the vacation unanimously by voice vote.

publicComment: Two speakers offered public comment, both regarding Yawkey Park landmarking. Kathy Foley read a written statement from five Yawkey family heirs supporting the landmark designation to protect the park's 106-year-old footprint for public use in perpetuity. Christine Martins, who authored the nomination, noted the Historic Preservation Commission had passed it unanimously and that no opposition had been raised at any prior public hearing.

title: Administrative Policy Committee and Village Board - Budget Workshop 2
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter held its second 2027 Budget Workshop covering public safety budgets (police and fire/EMS), TIF district updates, community development staffing, and a future debt service preview. The board's most significant action was recommending and approving keeping the contingency fund at $60,000 rather than the proposed $70,000, saving approximately $12 on a $200,000 home's village tax share. Village Administrator John Jacobs also previewed that the 2028 budget will likely require approximately a 20-cent tax rate increase to cover new debt service if the capital improvement program borrowing proceeds.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Comment
Budget Workshop Discussion - Historical Tax Rate Overview and Equalized Valuation
Port-a-Potty Budget Discussion and Vandalism Update
TIF District Administration Costs - Legal Guidance from Financial Advisor
Police Department Budget Presentation
Fire and EMS Department Budget Presentation

Contingency Fund Motion and Vote

discussions.item: Historical Tax Rate and Equalized Valuation Overview
discussions.body: Village Administrator John Jacobs presented a historical chart showing the village's assessed and equalized tax rates since 2020, noting that at full equalized valuation the rate would drop from $4.26 to approximately $2.71-$2.80. He contextualized the village's rate against Marathon County, two school districts, and NCTC, noting the village represents only about 20-25% of a resident's total tax bill. He noted Marathon County's rate of $3.48 is higher than the village's proposed rate.

discussions.item: Port-a-Potty Budget and Vandalism
discussions.body: Staff presented a cost chart for port-a-potty options ranging from approximately $6,700 for six standard units to over $21,000 with ADA-accessible units. Staff recommended a combination of three regular and three ADA units as a reasonable middle ground. Officials identified Bushka Park and Friendship Park as the primary vandalism sites, noting most damage occurs during daytime hours and that the contracted vendor has a policy of pulling units if vandalism occurs. No formal vote was taken; the matter was flagged for parks committee review.

discussions.item: TIF District Administration Costs - Legal Guidance
discussions.body: Jacobs reported receiving guidance from financial advisor Ariana Schmidt of Ehlers clarifying that administrative costs, professional services, and DOR fees can continue through the maximum life of a TID even after the expenditure period ends, but no new capital costs can be incurred after that period. Jacobs also disclosed a correction: TID 1 and TID 4 expenditure periods ended in 2019, not 2024 as previously documented. TID 2 had special legislation allowing expenditures through 2024. All three TIDs can continue accruing administrative costs until closure.

discussions.item: Police Department Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Police Chief Terry [last name inaudible] presented a largely status-quo budget, noting the primary cost increases stem from funding two officers for a full 12 months versus a partial year. A $21,700 line for new officer startup costs was removed. Capital equipment was cut by $9,000. The chief noted a planned hire is expected mid-to-late December at earliest, which could yield some payroll savings. Crossing guard pay was raised to $20/hour to aid retention. A $1,500 full-body restraint wrap system was requested as new equipment. The municipal court clerk overlap budget for Diane's retirement transition was also discussed, along with a proposed municipal judge salary increase from $5,500 to $6,000 effective April 2027.

discussions.item: Fire and EMS Department Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Fire Chief Teresa O'Brien presented a budget with modest increases, primarily for radio replacement ($20,000 from fire budget, $5,000 from EMS) and $800 in additional training. EMS call volume is projected at 492-500 for 2026-2027, up from 420 budgeted, a 25% increase driven largely by mental health-related calls. The EMS wage budget of $68,546 is expected to run approximately $9,000-$10,000 over, requiring a budget amendment in November. O'Brien highlighted three supplemental grant funds — 2% fire dues, FAP EMS grant (~$35,000/year), and a fire donations fund — totaling approximately $70,000 in non-general-fund expenditures annually.

discussions.item: Community Development Staffing and Planning Tech Position
discussions.body: Jacobs noted savings in 2026 due to the gap between Pete's departure and Nathan's hiring on August 3rd. The planning technician position, funded from April 2026, remains unfilled, creating roughly $30,000 in 2026 savings. Two interviews have been conducted with candidates who have GIS experience. Planning commission meetings are proposed to increase from 12 to 16 annually, and zoning board of appeals from 2 to 4 meetings, resulting in modest cost increases. A $10,000 placeholder for a potential TID 5 feasibility study was recommended to remain in the budget.

discussions.item: TIF District Tax Increment and Distribution Center Impact
discussions.body: Jacobs presented estimated tax increment figures: TID 1 at $212,000-$213,000 (down from $255,000 due to decreased equalized valuation), TID 2 over $1,034,000 (up from $954,000), and TID 4 at $147,000. He noted debt restructuring freed up $863,000 in principal for TID 2, accelerating its potential closure. Once the distribution center in TID 1 is fully built out, it is projected to generate an additional $444,000 in annual tax increment, potentially paying back the $2.8 million general fund advance well before the 2044 maximum life. The board discussed adding interest charges to the inter-fund advance, with Jacobs noting the LGIP rate (approximately 3.25-3.5%) could be used.

discussions.item: Capital Improvement Program Borrowing and 2028 Debt Service Preview
discussions.body: Jacobs walked the board through a preliminary debt service analysis for a proposed $1,950,000 borrowing (including closing costs) at an estimated 4.75% over 20 years, mirroring a September 2024 Rothschild borrowing. The analysis showed existing debt service could increase from approximately $735,000 levied in 2027 to approximately $873,000 in 2028, representing roughly a 20-cent tax rate increase. Jacobs stressed this does not affect the 2027 budget but will need to be planned for in 2028. He noted the village has no existing debt beyond 2033. Trustee [inaudible] suggested exploring bank financing similar to prior practice rather than bond issuance.

discussions.item: 2028 Budget Pros and Cons
discussions.body: Jacobs verbally presented a list of anticipated 2028 budget factors. Pros included: increased building permit revenue from new subdivisions, potential diesel price decrease eliminating the ~$30/household garbage fuel surcharge, higher highway aid formula funding from infrastructure investment, significantly higher net new construction valuation post-revaluation, no board salary overlap increases, reduced attorney fees as a goal, no three-month court clerk overlap cost, and no revaluation cost ($190,000/year savings). Cons included: projected sewer utility rate increase, deputy clerk moving to 12-month funding, four elections in a presidential year, higher building inspection costs, 20-cent debt service increase, and need to replenish the capital replacement fund.

discussions.item: Contingency Fund Vote
discussions.body: Guy Fidel moved to reduce the contingency fund from the proposed $70,000 to $30,000, arguing residents face hardship and a reduction would build board credibility. The motion failed for lack of a second. APC member Chris Clutes then moved to recommend keeping the contingency at $60,000, seconded by Mary Solheim; the APC recommendation passed. Erin Mishka then moved at the village board level to keep the contingency at $60,000, seconded by Solheim. The motion passed; Jacobs noted the reduction from $70,000 to $60,000 lowers the tax rate from $4.26 to $4.20 and saves approximately $12 on a $200,000 home's village portion.

publicComment: No public comment was offered.

title: Joint Budget Workshop Meeting
overview: The Village of Weston held a Joint Budget Workshop Meeting on Monday, October 19, 2026, reviewing the proposed 2027 budget across all funds and taking action on the refuse/recycling fee and the public hearing notice. The board approved a $30 increase in the annual garbage fee to $235.50 for 2027, and approved the 2027 budget public hearing notice (5-2) with a projected tax rate decrease of approximately 8 cents per thousand dollars of assessed value, setting a public hearing for November 16.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Comment
Approval of October 5, 2026 Joint Budget Workshop Meeting Minutes
Acknowledge Work Product Transmittals: September Budget Status Report, TIF 1 and TIF 2 Detail Reports, Legal Details for September
Unfinished Business: Review and Discussion of 2027 Budget (General Fund, Special Revenue Fund, Debt Service Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Utilities Fund)

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: One member of the public spoke, raising several concerns: the refuse fund reserve being depleted by fuel surcharges rather than direct billing; an estimated $100,000 in fuel surcharges being absorbed by the village without billing the Town of Weston for its approximately 5% share; a request to explain a tax rate chart on page 54 that he alleged was misleading because it reflected a property revaluation rather than actual spending reductions; and a question about why the Mountain Bay Metro Police Department budget showed a 4.63% increase when less than 3% was approved by the oversight board.

discussions.item: Approval of October 5, 2026 Joint Budget Workshop Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: Minutes were approved by both the Finance & Human Resources Committee and the Board of Trustees. Trustee Beck noted a correction: the minutes recorded her vote on a 6-to-1 motion as an aye but it should have been a nay. Staff confirmed the correction would be made.

discussions.item: Acknowledge Work Product Transmittals (September Budget Status Report, TIF Reports, Legal Details)
discussions.body: Each transmittal was acknowledged separately by the Finance & Human Resources Committee. During discussion of the September budget status report, Trustee Ermeling asked about the Board of Trustees line showing only about $38,000 spent against a $63,000 budget; staff explained the majority is wages with remaining accounts held for training and lodging that are not always used. Trustee Clark asked about interest income, and staff explained it derives from general fund bank accounts and investments. The legal details prompted a question about a $1,500 attorney cost related to an open records request; staff explained it was resolved with no further appeal pending.

discussions.item: Review and Discussion of 2027 Budget — General Fund
discussions.body: Staff reported the projected tax rate decrease had narrowed from 10 cents to approximately 8 cents per thousand after updated assessment ratio data arrived on Friday, with the assessment ratio dropping to 0.86, triggering a future reassessment obligation. Trustee Ermeling raised numerous line-item questions including DPW director salary moving back from TIF to the general fund, a street operations bonus incentive of $66,000 tied to transportation aid increases, the Mountain Bay PD budget showing a 4.63% increase due to a prior-year accounting restructuring rather than a true contract increase, and $8,000 in credit card fees for the aquatic center explained as fully offset by user fees. Trustee Beck asked about pool revenue being budgeted lower than current-year actuals; staff explained they average multiple years to avoid overestimating. Discussion arose about moving the $15,000 contingency salary line to the appropriate department budgets; staff explained it is kept in contingency because wage approvals are not finalized at budget time.

discussions.item: Review and Discussion of 2027 Budget — Special Revenue Funds, Debt, Capital, and Utilities
discussions.body: Staff noted TIF 1 is at zero and approximately $1.5 million will be allocated to taxing districts after the final audit. The farmers market budget increase from $18,000 to $25,000 was discussed and attributed to budgeting closer to actual historical expenditures. Extensive debt discussion ensued: Trustee Beck questioned whether the $4 million bank note for the Mountain Bay police building was included in the $49.38 million combined principal figure presented by the village's financial advisor; staff and Trustee Clark confirmed it was included after locating the orange-highlighted footnote in the advisor's Table 1. Trustees expressed concern about total village outstanding debt of approximately $55 million and the long-term sustainability of continued borrowing. Staff recommended bringing the village's debt policy (last reviewed in May 2008) back for board review early in the new year, and the board supported that direction. On utilities, staff flagged the need for a sanitary sewer rate increase in 2027, noting Remote Metro costs had grown by nearly $1 million over the prior decade in ways that were difficult to predict.

discussions.item: Refuse/Recycling Fund and Potential Increase in Garbage Fees
discussions.body: Staff presented options for increasing the annual garbage fee from $205.50, showing projected fund balances at $225, $230, and $235.50. The estimated fund balance at year-end 2026 is $62,400 and covers both village and town residents. Staff clarified the Town of Weston pays the same per-unit rate as village residents and is billed accordingly, disputing a public commenter's assertion that the town was not being charged its share of fuel surcharges. Trustee Rickert moved to set the fee at $235.50 for 2027 with a re-evaluation the following year; the Finance & Human Resources Committee approved unanimously. The Board of Trustees then approved the same recommendation; Trustee Olson voted nay.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Public Hearing Notice
discussions.body: Staff presented the proposed public hearing notice and noted the estimated assessed tax rate would be updated to approximately $5.52 per thousand. A motion to approve the notice with the updated rate was made and passed by the Finance & Human Resources Committee. The Board of Trustees then voted 5-2 to approve, with Trustees Clark and Beck voting nay. The public hearing was set for the November 16 board meeting.

publicComment: One member of the public spoke. He raised four concerns: (1) the refuse fund reserve is being depleted by fuel surcharges rather than by directly billing for the service, and the fund will be insolvent within months; (2) the Town of Weston is on the village's trash contract and subject to the same fuel surcharges but the village is not billing the town for its estimated $100,000 share, and he called on the board to include billing the town for its approximately 5% portion of 2026 surcharges and to bill monthly going forward; (3) a tax rate chart on page 54 appeared misleading because the dip shown for 2025 resulted from a property revaluation, not reduced spending, and he challenged staff to show a single-family home tax bill that actually decreased; (4) the Mountain Bay Metro Police Department budget showed a 4.63% increase while the oversight board approved less than 3%, and he asked where the additional money goes.

title: Public Health & Safety Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Public Health & Safety Committee voted unanimously to recommend striking the 2027-2028 Flock camera contract appropriations and directing the police to immediately cease using the surveillance cameras — a significant civil liberties decision driven by strong community opposition. The committee also received an impressive update on the city's Community Care Paramedic program, which has achieved a 63% reduction in 911 calls among enrolled patients, and discussed deer and feral cat management, a tavern shooting incident involving 100 demerit points, and the police department's third quarter report.

agenda.item: Return to open session — Flock camera contract vote
Community Care Paramedic program update (Item 6A)
Deer and feral cats within city limits (Item 6B)
Police department third quarter report (Item 6C)
Tavern activities report for August and September (Item 6D)
Adjournment (Item 7)

discussions.item: Flock Camera Contract — Cease Use and Strike Future Appropriations
discussions.body: Alder Solanski moved a two-part motion: refer to the Finance Committee to strike 2027 and 2028 Flock contract appropriations, and refer to the Common Council to direct the police department to immediately cease using Flock cameras and bag them so Flock cannot access them. Alder Trueblood expressed concern about breach of contract implications, noting the city's commitments should mean something. Alder Lukens voted in favor citing reports that Flock had reinstalled cameras in other municipalities after contracts were terminated. Alder Solanski explained the two-part structure addressed both financial liability and continued surveillance separately, noting the city had already spent $150,000 on the contract. A question arose about whether the Marathon County Sheriff's Department could still place Flock cameras on county roads within the city; city attorney indicated the county could place cameras on county property without city authorization. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Community Care Paramedic Program Update
discussions.body: Community Paramedic Matt Kozlowski (also referred to as Kosloski in self-introduction) presented an 8-minute condensed report on the program's first year and a half. The program has served approximately 50-70 patients and achieved a 63% reduction in 911 calls — 273 fewer calls — translating to an estimated $300,000 in avoided medical bills for vulnerable residents. Kozlowski shared case studies including an elderly veteran nearly evicted due to suspected dementia, a patient triple-dosing diabetes medication out of confusion, and an elderly woman repeatedly falling due to a broken sofa, all of whom received direct hands-on assistance. Alders Solanski and Lukens praised the program; Kozlowski noted he is currently the only community paramedic for Wausau and is working with Aspirus to expand to Stevens Point, Merrill, and Wisconsin Rapids.

discussions.item: Deer and Feral Cats Within City Limits
discussions.body: Alder Solanski raised the issue as her most frequently heard constituent complaint, noting uncertainty about what the city can actually do. Patrol Captain Melinda Pauls outlined existing options: archery hunting is permitted on private property and some city property with police department registration; the DNR has an online nuisance deer reporting portal; and the city could request additional deer tags from the DNR as Rib Mountain has done. On feral cats, Pauls noted three CSOs are still dedicated to animal control. The chair and Alder Solanski suggested publicizing existing ordinances against feeding wild animals through the city newspaper and improving the city website's usability for residents seeking quick animal-related guidance.

discussions.item: Police Department Third Quarter Report
discussions.body: Captain Pauls noted it was another busy quarter with a focus on mental health calls and high-risk calls. No specific figures were discussed in the meeting beyond what was included in the written packet. The committee had no questions and placed the report on file.

discussions.item: Tavern Activities Report — August and September / 100-Point Demerit Incident
discussions.body: Captain Pauls described an incident in which a gunshot victim arrived at Aspirus hospital and investigation traced the shooting to a Wausau bar. Surveillance video and witness statements — including one indicating a bartender announced shots fired to help patrons flee before police arrived — led to the establishment receiving 100 demerit points for failing to report the shooting. Alder Watson asked what demerit points mean; it was explained that at 100 points, the city sends a letter of concern and the establishment's owners are summoned to appear before the committee at the next meeting for the committee to determine penalties such as fines or license suspension. The committee confirmed the matter would appear on the next agenda. A 50-point violation at a venue called Intermission was noted but no action was taken, as the threshold for committee action is 100 points.

publicComment: No public comment was offered during the recorded portion of the meeting. However, Alder Solanski referenced strong community input received in preceding weeks opposing the Flock cameras, and the chair thanked the community for showing up to various meetings on the topic.

title: Tourism Commission
overview: The Village of Weston Tourism Commission met on October 19, 2026, acknowledging a strong summer tourism season highlighted by the World Horseshoe Tournament, which generated $3.2 million in direct visitor spending and $5.1 million in economic impact. Two grant requests — the 2026 Fall Cup post-event request and a tree-clearing project on the Eau Claire River — were tabled until the January 2027 meeting due to missing post-action reports and absent applicants. Several post-event reports were acknowledged and a suggestion was raised to require revenue/expense summaries in future post-event reporting.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Jim Pensel, 500 [street inaudible] Weston, raised two concerns: first, that the meeting packet layout was confusing; second, that a post-event request for the Fall Cup soccer event was submitted without a concurrent after-action report even though the event had already occurred. He also questioned the realism of room estimates in some applications, noting the Village of Weston only has 317 hotel rooms, and urged that future applications specify rooms impacted within Weston specifically.

discussions.item: September Budget Status Report
discussions.body: The commission acknowledged a budget status report showing revenues and expenditures through the second quarter. A member noted the account balance stood at $233,531. No questions were raised and the report was acknowledged by motion.

discussions.item: CVB Report
discussions.body: CVB representative Tim reported a highly successful summer tourism season, led by the World Horseshoe Tournament, which drew approximately 3,000 participants and families over two-plus weeks, generated $3.2 million in direct visitor spending and $5.1 million in economic impact, and brought hotel occupancy in the area to 86.2%. Tim noted discussions are underway with World Horseshoe leadership about potentially hosting again in 2033 and 2037 without a formal bid process. Marathon County's total annual tourism economic impact was cited at over $520 million with 2 million-plus visitors. Discussion also touched on the lack of new grant applications ahead of the upcoming funding cycle and whether posting meeting dates publicly on the CVB website would help applicants meet deadlines.

discussions.item: Grant Request — 2026 Fall Cup Post-Event Request
discussions.body: Commissioners noted applicant Dan was not present to explain the late submission. Tim confirmed the CVB had no communication from Dan regarding the application or his absence. Members expressed concern about setting a precedent by approving after-the-fact requests without adequate documentation, though several acknowledged the Fall Cup is a significant event. The commission voted unanimously to table the item until January, directing the CVB to contact Dan and require his presence at the next meeting along with a post-action report.

discussions.item: Grant Request — Clearing of Trees from Eau Claire River
discussions.body: The applicant was not present. One commissioner shared a personal account of a dangerous incident on the river caused by downed trees, supporting the safety rationale for the project, and noted the trees had already been cut. However, commissioners agreed they lacked sufficient detail — including how many trees were removed, photos, and a post-action report — to act. The item was tabled until January with a request for pictures and a full post-action report.

discussions.item: Post-Event Reports (Items 9A–9E): Wings over Wisconsin Wausau, Fourth of July, Weston Acoustic Concert Series, Bluesfest, World Horseshoe Tournament
discussions.body: Commissioners reviewed five post-event reports. Questions were raised about the Wings over Wisconsin Wausau report regarding what the 'value amount' column represented (clarified as marketing expenditures, not revenues) and whether the event's financials were disclosed. A suggestion was made to add a revenues-versus-expenses requirement to post-event reporting forms, with the chair directing this be placed as a separate action item for January. All five post-event reports were acknowledged by a single motion, passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Staff Remarks and Future Meeting
discussions.body: Staff reminded commissioners that a Halloween map is currently active for residents to submit Halloween activities, and that the end-of-year farmers market survey is open through October 30th. The next meeting was set for January 18th, 2027, at 4 p.m., with the two tabled grant items and a potential policy vote on post-event financial reporting to be added to the agenda.

He urged the commission to require applications to specify hotel rooms impacted within the Village of Weston specifically.

title: Board of Trustees
overview: The Village of Weston Board of Trustees met and addressed several significant items, including approving a 10-year fixed-rate loan at 4.95% for the new Mountain Bay Metro Police Department headquarters after the original lender submitted terms inconsistent with what the board had approved. The board also narrowly passed (4-3) a limited written public comment policy stating written comments will not be read aloud, after extended debate, and approved an early-start construction permit for footings and foundation at the new police station site. Three public commenters raised concerns about Kennedy Park finances, auditorium acoustics, and due diligence regarding a natural gas pipeline near the police station property.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Three residents spoke. Jim Pence criticized the lack of a financial plan for Kennedy Park (Miller Park North), called for canceling new lights and redirecting the $100,000 raised toward operating costs, and raised concerns about agenda item 42 — arguing the borrowing terms were inconsistent with what the court approved and that a 5-year balloon payment was never mentioned in the original August approval. John Alman complained that attendees in the back of the room cannot hear proceedings and suggested a simple microphone solution rather than spending on ball diamonds. Cynthia Russell expressed concern about lack of due diligence regarding a 36-inch TC Energy natural gas pipeline on or near the Mountain Bay Metro Police Station property, drew comparisons to the Camp Phillips development failure, and requested an independent survey, formal written engagement with TC Energy, and a written policy for future land purchases near utility easements.

discussions.item: Approval of September 21st Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: The minutes were approved with one requested correction: a trustee noted that language describing completed 'contracts for the chief and deputy' was misleading and should be reworded to reflect that union staffing contracts — not personal employment contracts — were completed. The administrator agreed to make the correction. Motion by Olson, second by Clark; approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Department Head Reports
discussions.body: Parks & Rec Director Sean reported the Kennedy Park community foundation account balance was updated, the Gold Games are scheduled again for 2027, and that the master plan needs revisiting since the farmers market is not relocating, which affects plans for an additional baseball field. Trustees discussed maintenance costs (reduced due to artificial turf), turf lifespan (10–20 years), and future capital costs. Planning & Development Director Jen reported on conference takeaways including data centers, solar, and conditional use permit practices; she also noted work underway to add farm stand regulations to code by spring. Police Chief reported 2,493 attendees at the Monster Bash and 596 traffic stops in the reporting month. Technology Director Nate reported an initial proposal of $69,000 for wireless microphones from one vendor and noted a second proposal was pending; trustees expressed sticker shock and discussed lower-cost alternatives including corded systems.

discussions.item: Discussion/Action on Draft Policy for Receipt and Handling of Written Comments at Public Hearings
discussions.body: Extended debate occurred over multiple provisions. Trustee Olson objected to a Wednesday noon deadline for written comments to be included in the packet, arguing submissions should be accepted the day of the meeting. Administrator Jamie clarified the policy was not designed to restrict submission but only to set packet inclusion deadlines, with later submissions handled as copies. An amendment by Trustee Clark to require that copies of written comments be made available to the public at the meeting table failed 5-2. The original motion to approve the policy as presented also failed 5-2. Trustee Ermeling then moved a simplified motion that written comments will not be read aloud; that motion passed 4-3 with Maloney, Lopes-Serrao, Ermeling, and Zeyghami voting yes, and Beck, Clark, and Olson voting no.

discussions.item: Discussion/Action on Proposed Site Plan Modifications and Early Start Permit — Mountain Bay Metro Police Station
discussions.body: Staff explained that a revised site plan was needed after the TC Energy natural gas pipeline easement required the building footprint to shift westward; the new site plan is outside the pipeline easement, with parking lot crossings approved by TC Energy. The board was asked to authorize staff to issue an early start permit limited to footings and foundation, with final amended site plan approval deferred to the November board meeting. Staff noted the revised layout may actually cost less due to reduced asphalt and removal of a door and sidewalk. Motion passed 4-3 with Beck, Olson, and Ermeling voting no.

discussions.item: Discussion/Action on Engineering Design Contract — Bowman Street Water and Sanitary Sewer Replacement
discussions.body: The board approved awarding the design contract for water and sanitary sewer utility replacements on Bowman Street between Business 51 and McIntyre to Becker Hobby for $22,500. Trustees confirmed this was design only, not the full construction project. Motion by [inaudible], second by Zeyghami; approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Discussion/Action on Engineering Services Contract Amendment — Business 51 Storm Pond Construction Project
discussions.body: The board approved an engineering contract amendment with Strand Associates for construction oversight related to a clean water fund loan through the DNR for a regional storm pond project serving Weston, Rothschild, and Schofield. Trustee Clark questioned why the state DOT had no financial stake given that state highway runoff flows to the pond; Public Works Director Michael acknowledged ongoing frustration with the DOT's position that they are not subject to the same phosphorus removal requirements. The village's cost share was noted as approximately 80%. Motion by Zeyghami, second by Lopes-Serrao; approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Discussion/Action on Debt for Village of Weston Portion of New Police Headquarters
discussions.body: Administrator Jamie explained that Community First/Inner City bank had submitted loan documents with a 5-year balloon or rate reset, inconsistent with the board's prior approval of a 10-year fixed rate at 4.69%. After negotiations, the bank offered a fourth option: 10-year fixed at 4.95%. Trustees discussed the risk of the balloon/reset options given uncertain future interest rates and concluded the 4.95% 10-year fixed was the best path forward. Trustee Olson moved to accept the 10-year fixed rate at 4.95%, seconded by Clark; approved unanimously. Finance Director noted $400,000 already levied for debt service would immediately reduce the principal upon issuance.

publicComment: Three residents spoke. Jim Pence criticized the lack of a financial strategy for Kennedy Park ongoing costs, called for canceling new lights to redirect funds, and challenged the debt terms for the police station loan as inconsistent with court-approved terms. John Alman complained the public cannot hear board proceedings from the back of the room and suggested an inexpensive microphone solution. Cynthia Russell raised detailed concerns about insufficient due diligence regarding a TC Energy natural gas pipeline near the proposed police station site, compared it to a prior Camp Phillips development failure, and requested an independent pipeline survey, written engagement with TC Energy, and a formal utility verification policy for future land purchases.

title: Police & Fire Commission
overview: The Wausau Police & Fire Commission held a brief meeting that included dismissal of a citizen complaint reconsideration, followed by presentations from police and fire department leadership on budget proposals, recruitment, and technology updates. Key topics included proposed 2027 budget cuts for both departments, an active police recruitment process targeting 8-10 new hires, fire department apprentice program updates, and an informational presentation on the Flock Safety automated license plate reader (ALPR) system ahead of a public health and safety committee meeting that evening.

agenda.item: Motion to dismiss reconsideration of citizen complaint of JV

discussions.item: Dismissal of citizen complaint reconsideration (JV)
discussions.body: The meeting opened with a motion to dismiss the reconsideration of a citizen complaint identified only as 'JV.' The motion was made and seconded without debate, and was approved by voice vote. No discussion of the complaint's substance was recorded.

discussions.item: Wausau Police Department 2027 Budget Overview
discussions.body: In Chief Barnes's absence, a deputy chief-level official presented the proposed 2027 police budget. Key changes include ending the All Cities Management contract for adult crossing guards (saving ~$40,000), cutting the CSO budget by 50% (~$45,000 savings), maintaining the humane society non-dog stray contract at $18,500, restructuring the SRO contract to seek 100% school-year coverage by the district (~$50,000 savings), and reducing authorized sworn staff from 81 to 80 as foundation funding for the downtown officer program phases out. The city council also approved a $50,000 feasibility study into the UW-Stevens Point campus as a potential future police and fire facility.

discussions.item: Police Recruitment Update
discussions.body: Captain Pauls reported that a recruitment process launched in August drew just over 40 applicants, down sharply from approximately 400 applicants 25 years ago, though the quality of candidates was described as strong. The department is hiring 8 to 10 officers to address current vacancies and four anticipated retirements in early 2025. Twelve background investigations are currently underway, with at least three candidates expected to be brought to the commission at a special November 5th PFC meeting, as some candidates are also considering other departments.

discussions.item: Flock Safety ALPR System Update
discussions.body: Captain Graham provided an update on the department's Flock Safety automated license plate reader program, which has been before committee or council approximately seven or eight times since a contract was signed in 2023. He illustrated the system's reactive and proactive capabilities with a retail theft case in which ALPR identified a suspect vehicle, linked it to over $5,000 in additional thefts, and enabled a traffic stop while the suspect was returning to commit another theft. A commission member raised privacy concerns about potential misuse by officers or third parties, particularly in domestic violence situations; Captain Graham explained that public access to the system is not possible, that officer access requires multi-factor authentication, and that the system is CJIS compliant with monthly and annual audits. A transparency portal on the department's website was noted. The chair reminded the commission that its jurisdiction is largely limited to hiring, discipline, and investigations, making the discussion informational in nature.

discussions.item: Fire Department 2027 Budget and Hiring Update
discussions.body: Fire Chief [name not stated in transcript] reported that proposed 2027 budget cuts are achieved primarily by leaving the Division Chief of Training position—vacant since January 2025—open until July 1, 2027, and leaving a second position in the inspection bureau open for six months following an upcoming retirement. On hiring, the department interviewed two candidates in closed session earlier that day and had three more interviews scheduled that afternoon, with an additional application received the prior Friday. Nine new firefighter apprentices began three weeks prior and are now on 48-hour shifts while attending NTC two to three days per week.

discussions.item: Fire Department Succession Planning
discussions.body: The fire chief described plans to present a revised organizational chart to HR and the finance department before year-end, aimed at building redundancy and succession pathways. A key element would formally integrate the community care paramedic position under the EMS Division Chief, given that roughly 80% of city calls are EMS-related and the division currently has limited leadership redundancy. The chief noted a Lieutenant promotion interview will also need to be scheduled, potentially requiring a special December PFC meeting.

publicComment: No public comment was offered during this meeting, though a reference was made to prior public comment from a citizen who mentioned concerns about a stalker in the context of the Flock Safety discussion.

The commission then approved minutes from the prior meeting and moved into closed session to interview candidates for firefighter/paramedic and police detective positions, as well as to consider a citizen complaint reconsideration request.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Flock License Plate Reader System
discussions.body: Three residents spoke during public comment, all raising concerns about the Flock automated license plate reader (ALPR) system. Felix Gallow presented data alleging widespread surveillance abuse and called on the commission to close data sharing with outside agencies, limit search access to supervisors, require case IDs for every search, and overhaul the audit process. Courtney Olsen, also of 1206 Highland Park Boulevard, identified herself as a domestic violence advocate and police trainer, asking the commission to use its oversight role to request a report on arrests and convictions tied to Flock data, an audit of outside-agency searches, and the department's own camera location list before the city council votes on the $50,000 budget item. Mary CL of 127 Kent Street spoke as a concerned neighbor, citing personal experience with a stalker and expressing discomfort with private companies collecting movement data on residents without clear data security guarantees. The chair acknowledged the comments and noted the topic would be discussed during adjournment.

discussions.item: Consideration of Minutes from Preceding Meeting
discussions.body: A commissioner requested a clarification on page five of the minutes regarding a fire/EMS audit reference to two agencies listed as 'USDA' and 'DEA,' asking which agency conducted the audit and that acronyms be spelled out. The chair confirmed the audit was conducted by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) and directed that correction be made. The minutes were then approved with that correction on a voice vote.

discussions.body: The commission voted to enter closed session under Wisconsin State Statute 19.85(1)(c) to interview two candidates for firefighter/paramedic with the Wausau Fire Department and one candidate for promotion to detective with the Wausau Police Department, and under 19.85(1)(f) to consider a reconsideration request regarding the dismissal of a citizen complaint identified as JV. The motion passed on a voice vote.

publicComment: Three speakers addressed the commission, all on the topic of the Flock license plate reader system. Felix Gallow cited research on surveillance abuse and made four specific policy recommendations. Courtney Olsen, a domestic violence advocate and police trainer, asked the commission to request accountability data from the police department before budget decisions are finalized. Mary CL spoke as a private citizen concerned about privacy, data security, and the potential for stalkers or other bad actors to access Flock data.

title: Administrative Policy Committee and Village Board - Budget Workshop 1
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter held its first budget workshop for the 2027 fiscal year on October 19, 2026, with joint participation from the Administrative Policy Committee and Village Board. Village Administrator John and Finance Director Jim presented a comprehensive budget overview proposing a 5.7% tax rate increase (from $4.03 to $4.26 per $1,000 assessed value), a 6.99% levy increase to $2.9 million, and a $30 garbage fee surcharge due to diesel fuel costs, with the combined residential impact estimated at $62–$97 annually. No formal votes were taken; the session was a discussion and review workshop with a second session planned for October 20.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Comment
Budget Workshop Overview - Tax Levy and Tax Rate
Water and Sewer Rates Discussion
Department Budget Overviews - General Government, Village Board, Attorney, Municipal Court
Police Department Budget
Fire and EMS Budget
Public Works, Parks, and Community Development Budgets
General Fund Revenue Overview and Fund Balance Discussion

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: One member of the public, Bernie Kramer, spoke during public comment. He expressed concern about the village moving away from municipal water service toward private wells and septic systems in new residential development, arguing this would hurt utility revenue (90% of which comes from residential users), increase costs for future homeowners, and undermine the village's own long-range planning within the septic service area utility.

discussions.item: Tax Levy and Tax Rate
discussions.body: Village Administrator John presented a proposed tax rate increase from $4.03 to $4.26 per $1,000 assessed value, a 5.7% increase, and a levy increase from $2.7 million to $2.9 million (6.99%, approximately $190,000). He noted the village could legally levy as high as $4 million and a rate of $5.87 but was proposing well below that maximum. Trustee Mary Solheim raised concern that a 7% levy increase is unsustainable given only 0.651% net new construction, and staff acknowledged this while pointing to incoming developments (Green Tree, FAA property, TID 1 distribution center) as reasons for optimism.

discussions.item: Garbage Fee Surcharge
discussions.body: Staff proposed a $30 garbage fee increase per household attributable entirely to a diesel fuel surcharge from Harter's contract, triggered when diesel exceeds $4 per gallon. The village has been absorbing roughly $6,000 per month in extra fuel costs since March 2026 (approximately $60,000 total) from contingency reserves and TID III closure revenues. Staff recommended the surcharge remain until diesel prices drop below $4, at which point it would be removed. The base rate increase of $9.12 previously planned was set aside in favor of this surcharge-only approach.

discussions.item: Water and Sewer Rates
discussions.body: Staff reported no proposed rate increases for water or sewer in 2027. A 2.5% sewer rate increase had been anticipated for January 2027 tied to a borrowing, but the borrowing was delayed, pushing the first debt service payment to 2028. A new water well and water tower are planned but unlikely to be funded until 2028 or later, pending PSC review. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Police Department Budget
discussions.body: A second new officer budgeted for Q4 2026 will not be hired this year due to a thin applicant pool; Chief Terry plans to wait for a stronger candidate pool, possibly December academy graduates. Both new officers will be fully funded for 12 months in 2027. Health insurance for the police union came in at 14.2% increase (down from an initial 17% quote). Staff are exploring moving police union employees to the TeamCare plan to reduce per-employee health costs, with the union reportedly not opposed. Crossing guard pay was proposed to increase from $16.48 to $20 per hour due to recruitment difficulties.

discussions.item: Fire and EMS Budget
discussions.body: EMS ambulance runs are tracking at approximately 492 for 2026 against a budget of 420, and staff are projecting up to 500 runs for 2027, up from 390 actual in 2025. Administrator John said this requires a budget adjustment for 2026 and elevated funding in 2027. The Riverside formula for billing runs does not change for 2027 but includes a 1% increase effective 2028.

discussions.item: Public Works Budget
discussions.body: The road maintenance budget is proposed to increase from $386,000 to $400,000 (3.63%), roughly in line with CPI at 3.7%. Winter plow blades are up $5,000 and road salt is up approximately $8,000. Marathon County landfill tipping fees are increasing about $7,000. The grader lease payment was already reduced by $4,000 after a prior board-approved trade-in. State highway aid to the village increased $52,000 (the maximum 15% allowed) due to increased infrastructure spending, including the Kronenwetter Drive project.

discussions.item: Community Development and Planning Tech Position
discussions.body: Staff reported they are close to making an offer to a planning technician candidate to assist Planning Director Nathan. The position was only funded for nine months in 2026; it will be funded for a full 12 months in 2027. Administrator Jim emphasized urgency in hiring given high foot traffic at village hall for zoning questions and incoming development activity.

discussions.item: TID 1 Expenditure Period - Trustee Challenge
discussions.body: Trustee Dan Lesniak raised a concern that it may not be legally permissible to make new expenditures from TID 1 because its expenditure period has ended, except potentially for administration costs. Administrator John said auditors and financial advisor Ehlers had previously indicated administration costs, assessment costs, and audit costs can flow through, but agreed to confirm the question definitively at the next night's meeting.

discussions.item: General Fund Revenue Overview
discussions.body: Staff identified several revenue improvements: shared revenue up about $10,000 (2%); a $54,000 annual Magellan termination payment that had never been budgeted previously; highway aid up $52,000; and building permits trending up from $40,000 budget to an estimated $60,000. Cable franchise fee revenue is declining significantly, estimated at $60,500 for 2027 versus a prior budget of $90,000, attributed to residents switching to streaming services. Total general fund revenue is proposed to increase approximately $657,000 or 11%, with fund balance drawdowns for one-time items including $90,000 for year two of the revaluation, $75,000 for municipal building CIP projects, and a $10,000 carryover for potential TID 5 creation work.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Bernie Kramer. He criticized the village for allowing new residential development to proceed with private wells and septic systems rather than connecting to municipal water and sewer, arguing this undermines utility revenue, increases long-term costs for homeowners, and contradicts the village's own planning documents. He also criticized what he characterized as illogical decision-making and the reduction in lot count in some developments.
actionItems: Staff to confirm with Ehlers financial advisors whether administration-related expenditures from TID 1 are permissible after the expenditure period has ended, and report back at the October 20 budget workshop
Police Chief Terry to provide data on crossing guard pay rates in comparable communities
Staff to explore moving police union employees to the TeamCare health insurance plan and report results; changes may be incorporated on the night of budget adoption if logistics align
Staff to publish the proposed budget by end of the week or early the following week to start the required two-week public review period before November adoption

Planning Director Nathan to proceed toward making an offer to a planning technician candidate
Second budget workshop session scheduled for October 20, covering TIF districts, public safety (police and fire), and community development in detail

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held its October 19, 2026 meeting with only four of seven members present — a bare quorum. The commission approved a zoning change and certified survey map for a residential parcel split on Aspen Road, but voted to postpone action on a controversial conditional use permit for a non-metallic mine at 1320 Kowalski Road, citing the reduced commission membership and the significance of the decision.

agenda.item: Call to Order and Pledge of Allegiance
Roll Call
Public Hearing: Conditional Use Permit — Oakley River LLC / Eau Claire River LLC, 1320 Kowalski Road (non-metallic mine)
Public Hearing: Zoning Change Request — Gene Pachinsky, 3115 Aspen Road (RR5 to RR2)
Public Comment (general)
Community Development Director Report — Nathan Sandwick
New Business: Certified Survey Map — Gene Pachinsky, 3115 Aspen Road
New Business: Zoning Change Request — Gene Pachinsky, 3115 Aspen Road

discussions.item: Public Hearing: Conditional Use Permit — Eau Claire River LLC, Non-Metallic Mine at 1320 Kowalski Road
discussions.body: Multiple speakers addressed the commission. Guy Fridell, a longtime advocate for a Kowalski Road interchange, strongly opposed the permit, arguing it would undermine decades of village planning and investment, conflict with the comprehensive plan, and that the economic benefits of the interchange — 1,000–1,200 jobs and $100–125 million in new tax base — far outweigh speculative benefits from sand mining. Tom Redens, representing applicant Eau Claire River LLC with Gary Gert and Kurt Sebert, argued the mine would allow the flood-prone site to be graded to a buildable pad and that the village board had already voted months earlier to abandon the interchange committee, making the mine plan the viable path forward for TID-1 development. Neighbors Rich Barker, Dawn Barker (who raised concerns about fish — including walleye — in the existing pond), Dale Champagne, and others also spoke. A public commenter questioned the source of the projected 1,200 jobs and flood storage development challenges.

discussions.item: New Business: Zoning Change Request — Gene Pachinsky, 3115 Aspen Road (RR5 to RR2)
discussions.body: Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick explained the request: Pachinsky wants to split an 11-acre parcel so the 2.89-acre portion containing the existing home can be sold, but that parcel is too small for RR5 zoning. The commission discussed road frontage (118 feet, deemed sufficient) and the dead-end, low-traffic nature of Aspen Road. Trustee Stowell moved to recommend approval to the village board; Terry Lewis-Burkett seconded. The motion carried 4-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: New Business: Certified Survey Map — Gene Pachinsky, 3115 Aspen Road
discussions.body: The commission considered approval of the CSM contingent on the village board enacting the zoning change to RR2. Sandwick clarified the plan commission — not the village board — approves CSMs of this type. Trustee Stowell moved approval contingent on the zoning change; Terry Lewis-Burkett seconded. The motion carried 4-0 on roll call.

discussions.item: New Business: Conditional Use Permit — Eau Claire River LLC, 1320 Kowalski Road
discussions.body: After the public hearing, commissioners expressed reluctance to act with only four of seven members present on such a significant matter. Rick Grundman moved to postpone action; Trustee Stowell seconded. Commissioners noted a 60-day window from the public hearing to render a decision and agreed a special meeting would be scheduled. The postponement motion carried 4-0. Commissioners encouraged absent members to listen to the recorded public hearing testimony before the next meeting.

discussions.item: Community Development Director Report
discussions.body: Nathan Sandwick highlighted the recent zoning workshop, upcoming Green Tree Trail subdivision final plat review, a potential public hearing on private sewage disposal system ordinance changes, and his attendance at the Wisconsin APA conference. He also flagged a new state law requiring more specificity in comprehensive plans regarding residential growth areas, with compliance required before January 2028 — recommending the village update its plan before that deadline.

discussions.item: Zoning Code Review
discussions.body: The commission briefly discussed the zoning code review but deferred substantive discussion to the November 16th regular meeting due to the late hour and small attendance. Sandwick noted new state legislation allowing residential TIDs with smaller maximum lot sizes, which could require zoning code amendments if the village wishes to participate. A commissioner requested that someone with expertise on flood storage districts present at a future meeting to help commissioners better understand how flood storage, fill requirements, and development interact.

publicComment: No general public comment was offered during the public comment period. However, multiple speakers testified during the public hearing on the Eau Claire River LLC conditional use permit: Guy Fridell opposed the permit at length, citing interchange planning history and economic impact studies; Tom Redens of Land Planning Services spoke on behalf of the applicant; Rich Barker spoke in opposition (brief); Dale Champagne asked a clarifying question about the acreage to be mined; Dawn Barker raised a concern about fish, including walleye, currently in the existing pond; and an unidentified speaker asked where the projected 1,200 jobs would come from. No speakers addressed the Pachinsky zoning change public hearing.

Village to begin comprehensive plan updates for residential growth area specificity before December 31, 2027 compliance deadline

title: Board Educational Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held an educational meeting on October 15, 2026, primarily focused on a detailed presentation of Phase 4 construction plans for the proposed county highway facility, including a guaranteed maximum price of approximately $54.98 million. The board also previewed upcoming voting items for the next meeting, including multiple town rezoning ordinances, ARPA fund reallocation, and a land purchase near Cherokee Park. No formal votes were taken at this educational meeting, as action items are deferred to the October 20 HR Finance and Property Committee meeting and the subsequent full County Board meeting.

agenda.item: Pledge of Allegiance, moment of silent reflection, reading of notice, roll call
Public comment period (no speakers)
Standing committee announcements — Supervisor Robinson previews upcoming HR Finance and Property Committee agenda items
Review of upcoming ordinances: Town rezoning items (9A1–9A8)
Review of upcoming resolutions: Solid waste tipping policy, town wind/solar/data center ordinances (9B1–9B2C)
Review of upcoming resolutions: ARPA fund reclassification, imprest funds, tax deed property sales, Cherokee Park land purchase, pontoon boat donation (9B3A–9B3F)
Educational presentation: Phase 4 construction of proposed County Highway Facility — site plan, floor plans, geothermal HVAC, value engineering, air quality, and cost overview
Review of upcoming Infrastructure Committee resolutions: Crash Responder Safety Week, County Road Q property transfer (9B4A–9B4B)
Announcements and adjournment

discussions.item: Standing Committee Announcements
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson announced the HR Finance and Property Committee would meet the following Tuesday before the full County Board meeting, with the agenda including funding for the highway facility resolution, a resolution declaring November as Project Greenlight Month for veterans, and a resolution expressing concerns about proposed U.S. Census rule changes that could reduce Wisconsin's congressional representation by counting winter residents in southern states.

discussions.item: Town Wind, Solar, and Data Center Ordinances (9B2A–9B2C)
discussions.body: Supervisor Lemmer raised concerns about the county's shift to a purely compliance-based review of town ordinances rather than substantive legal review, questioning whether this created liability risk. Corporation counsel explained the shift was intended to limit the county's liability since towns that have opted out of county zoning must enforce their own ordinances; the county's role under state statute is only to verify procedural compliance. Supervisor Sandowski asked whether the Town of Wausau data center ordinance addressed hyperscale facilities, and was reminded that the town's ordinance applies only within its own boundaries.

discussions.item: Cherokee Park Land Purchase (Resolution 66-26)
discussions.body: Supervisor Jensen asked about the status of Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Fund funding referenced in the resolution; Administrator Landon and Supervisor Robinson explained there is currently no funding in the program but the reference was included so the county could pursue it if reauthorized. Supervisors Hagen and Jensen asked about the need for the land, its tax impact, and ongoing maintenance costs; Parks Director Jamie Paully explained the parcel is currently forested, generates minimal tax revenue, and would complete the park boundary along the river with minimal added maintenance unless future trail development is pursued.

discussions.item: Phase 4 Highway Facility Construction Presentation
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator and Facilities Director Chris Holman led an extensive presentation alongside project architect Ned Dirksen, Miron project executive Eric Brandt, and Excel Engineering's Corey Powers on geothermal HVAC, air quality filtration, value engineering savings, site and floor plans, and the guaranteed maximum price of $53.3 million in direct construction costs, with a total project figure of $54,980,537 including contingencies, design fees, and owner FF&E. Supervisors asked detailed questions about geothermal maintenance costs, MERV filter expenses, coal dust impacts on workers and equipment, backup heating systems, truck traffic flow, expansion capacity, LEED-equivalent design standards, and the competitive bid process; Holman and the project team answered that the bore field cost $1.9 million with a $760,000 IRA tax credit anticipated, that backup gas boilers are included for temperatures below zero, and that the guaranteed maximum price represents a ceiling with potential to come down. Supervisor Griner asked what percentage of the building would be immediately utilized, and Commissioner [inaudible] confirmed that all existing equipment including 82 large pieces, 24 plow trucks, and over 100 small tools would fill the main building, with current equipment routinely stored outside and degrading. The board was informed the resolution authorizing Phase 4 will be considered at the HR Finance and Property Committee on October 20 and then the full County Board that same evening.

publicComment: No public comment was offered.
actionItems: HR Finance and Property Committee to consider highway facility Phase 4 construction resolution (Resolution authorizing ~$54.98M project) on October 20
